content.content:
# The report and the record

## What every report holds

Your brief says where your report goes: a file that it names, your final message, or both. If it names no file, your report is your final message.

A finding is something that your work learned about the tree or the language, and that the record does not hold yet. Examples: a defect, a behaviour that departs from the specification or from a decision of the curator, a measurement. What you did along the way is not a finding, for example the files that you read or edited. Your transcript keeps that.

A fact is a finding that is an established property of the tree, the language, the library or their tools, and that later work builds on. A defect also gets its ledger row, and a fact about it may cite the row.

A point to report is a kind of change or finding that the curator wants to review. Your brief names its points to report. Examples: a changed line of a test that the team wrote, a checker edit inside a change to the library, a changed line of the model program.

Put each of these that you have in your report, in this form, whatever else your brief asks for:

- **Defects.** Each defect that you measured, and the test or ledger row that records it (`tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded").
- **Sentences of the specification made false.** Each sentence of the specification that your change makes false, quoted with its file and line. Such a sentence says what walk or the compiled path does. It is in the effect of an Appendix I entry (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex`), or in a `\revision` or `\note{}` box beside a passage.
- **Decisions.** Each choice that you made among alternatives, as a decision apart from the findings: what you chose, the alternatives, and the evidence, cited. If no decision of the curator covers it, say so, and say which reading you acted on. A decision left as a line inside the findings counts as not made.
- **Points to report.** Each point that your brief names and the work reached, with its evidence, also one that only part of the work reached.
- **For FACTS.** Each fact that your work established, in the hand-over form of "Writing to the record". If your brief let you write FACTS, give instead the number of each entry that you added or rewrote. If your work established no fact, write "none".
- **Commands.** Each command that you had to work out because this skill does not give it, with what it does.
- **Questions for the curator.** If something needs the curator's decision, list it as a decision not taken, in the form that `exploring.md` gives. The reader of your report brings it to the curator. Do not choose which of your items anyone reviews.

## At a point to report

- If the work reaches a point to report, do what the brief says for it. For example, a brief can say that a defect in the code is recorded in a ledger row and not repaired.
- Then finish the work.
- If a step cannot be undone, or would change a decision of the curator, report it instead. List it as a decision not taken, with its alternatives.

## Timings and citations

- If you take a timing that you will keep, run nothing else beside it. All agents of the session share the machine's cores (the `cloud-container` skill).
- Name the machine with every timing: `nproc`, the CPU's model and MHz, the load at start, the JDK, `FORTRESS_THREADS`. Only a pair of timings taken in one run measures a difference.
- If you take a measurement again because the code changed, say what changed.
- In a report, cite the tree at file:line, and quote results, two to five lines, each with its command. Never cite a file under `tmp/`.

## POSITIONS and FACTS

POSITIONS and FACTS describe the present: no dates, no names of who found what, no "corrected" or "superseded" notes. The history of each entry is in `POSITIONS-history.md` and `FACTS-history.md`, beside them. When your work needs the detail of an entry, print the report section that it cites (`$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'`, below). Read its history only when the tree disagrees with the entry.

Each entry is one line that starts with its permanent number: `F-87` in FACTS, `P-48` in POSITIONS. A FACTS entry is the fact as it stands now, what it means for the work, and the test that fails if the fact stops holding, under a bold title. If no test checks the fact, the entry gives the command and the output that show it. It points to the report section that holds the detail. Cite an entry by its number. If the reader must know what the entry says without printing it, add the first words of its title in quotes: F-87, "The first words ...".

## The gap ledger

The ledger's rows are the bug reports that the work fixes. A fix of a row starts with its reproduction, written as a test (`tests-writing.md`).

A row is one line of eight cells, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of a topic section. Reports cite a row by its number, which it keeps for good. A new issue gets a new row.

- Its status is one of seven words: `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`, `CONTESTED`, `RETIRED`, `FIXED`, `DUPLICATE`. The last three close a row. The row template (below) defines each.
- Its class is a kind and an area, such as `implementation gap (checker)`.
- The earlier text of a changed row is in `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger-history.md`.

Read the ledger only through the queries below: it is too large to read whole.

A row states its gap as it stands now. A note adds a fact. If your work changes what a row says, write the row's whole new line with `rewrite` (below), not a note that tells the repair.

The heading reader of `ledger.py` does not expand the specification's `\Trait{X}` macro. So a row that names a library trait's section cites `Specification-1.0-frozen/` by line.

## Reading the record

Read only the slice of the record that you need. This tool prints whole entries, in parts of bounded size:

    T=explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh

- `$T 'F-87'` prints one entry by its number, and `$T 'P-48'` one of POSITIONS. `$T 'F-87+'` adds each entry that F-87 cites by its number, and each entry that cites F-87. `$T 'history:F-87'` prints its history. Run one when your brief or a note cites an entry by its number.
- `$T 'positions:WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints one of the curator's decisions. Run it before you choose among ways to do something. If several titles hold the words, it names them.
- `$T 'WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints each FACTS entry whose bold title holds them, and `$T 'section:HEADING'` every entry of a FACTS section. Run one before you investigate a behaviour of the tree, and when your brief or a note names an entry. These queries and `positions:` read titles only: before you write that the record does not hold something, also grep FACTS and POSITIONS for its words.
- `$T 'index:WORDS'` prints the INDEX lines that hold the words. Run it to find the notes on a topic.
- `$T 'ledger-find:WORDS'` prints one line for each ledger row that holds every word. Run it when you meet a defect, before you investigate it.
- `$T 'ledger:ROW'` prints one row whole. Run it for each row that you need from a find, your brief or a note.
- `$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'` prints a section of any note, or of a `.tex` chapter, and `$T 'map:FILE#HEADING'` a section of a note under `explorations/coordinator/map/`. Run one when your brief or a note names a section. `#HEADING@WORDS` prints only the table rows and list items of that section that hold every one of WORDS.
- `$T --check QUERY ...` prints only where each query matches and its size. Run it before a query whose size you do not know. `--part N` prints part N of a long output, and `--help` gives the rest.

A word of a query that ends in `*` matches the start of a word. Any other word matches a whole word.

Before you edit a file of the original tree, list the ledger rows that cite it, and read each row that your edit can change:

    python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py find --cites FILE

## Writing to the record

- Write FACTS and POSITIONS only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`, never by hand. `add` gives a new entry its number, and `set` rewrites an entry. The tool writes the entry to `FACTS.md` or `POSITIONS.md`, and its earlier text to the history file beside it. It commits nothing: commit both files in one commit. Its header gives its usage.
- If your brief lets you write FACTS, add each fact as a new entry in the section of its topic, in the commit that establishes it. Put its detail in a section of your report: the file:line citations, the commands with their output, and the measured numbers. Point the entry to that section, by your report's file and the section's heading. If your report is only your final message, hand the fact over instead. Spend no effort on the entry's wording: it is rewritten to the record's form after your work.
- If your brief does not let you write FACTS, hand each fact over in the "For FACTS" item of your report, with:
  - the fact as it stands now, in one sentence;
  - what it means for the work;
  - the number that a decision rests on, if any, with what it counts; if its parts belong to different ledger rows, the part of each row;
  - the test that fails if the fact stops holding, or the command and the output that show it;
  - the section of your report that holds the detail.
- If your brief lets you write FACTS, rewrite a wrong entry in place. Otherwise say in your hand-over that the entry is wrong, with the evidence.
- POSITIONS holds each of the curator's decisions, in one place. Everything else points there. Write a decision there only if your brief gives it to you to record. If you have evidence against one, do as `exploring.md` says.
- Put new files of the work under `explorations/`. If you add a note directly in `explorations/` or `explorations/reviews/`, add its line to INDEX: ``- `PATH`: `` and the first sentence of the note's header comment.

Write the gap ledger only with `ledger.py`, which checks each line that it writes against the row template.

    L="python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py"

To add a row:

1. Print the row template, about 3 KB: `$T 'doc:explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md#The row template'`.
2. Write the row as one line in a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with `?` in its number cell.
3. Run `$L add FILE --section TITLE`. It numbers the row and puts it in that section. If the row breaks the template, it adds nothing and prints each rule broken. `$L sections` lists the titles.

To change a row:

- `$L note N TEXT` adds TEXT to the notes of row N. It refuses a note that takes the row past 1,200 characters, or its notes cell past 700 characters.
- `$L rewrite N FILE` replaces row N with the whole line in FILE, a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with N or `?` in its number cell. Use it to correct the claim, cut the notes or change the reproducer. The tool checks the line against the template and keeps the old line in the history file.
- `$L duplicate N --of M` makes row N a pointer to row M.
- `$L close N --commit HASH --test NAME` marks row N `FIXED`, by the commit HASH and its test NAME. Run it once that commit is in `HEAD`, and commit the close after it. NAME can also be a file under `explorations/coordinator/tools/`, or `none` with `--note REASON`. For a `CONTESTED` row, add `--settled TEXT`, which names what settled its question.
- `$L landing-check BASE` prints each problem, and exits 1 on any. Run it when your brief asks for it. It checks the whole ledger against the template, so a broken row that BASE already had counts too. The problems are a row that breaks the template, an `XXX` test deleted or renamed while a row that is not closed names it, a row that is not closed though a commit says it fixed it, and a FACTS or POSITIONS entry that disagrees with a row's status.

## The repository's history

- The repository is a 2018 fork of `sirinath/fortress`, a git conversion of the project's java.net Mercurial repository. Its trunk runs from 2007-01-04 to 2012-08-31 and ends at `a874948ac`, the team's last commit.
- The commits after `a874948ac` are the revival's. After the tag `sealed-tree`, commit `75cca6683`, the revival began to fix the team's code, test first. Before it, the revival changed mainly the build and the toolchain.
- `git diff a874948ac -- FILE` shows what the revival changed in a file, and `git diff 75cca6683 -- FILE` what it changed after the tag.
- The conversion cut 146 parent links, so a `git log` of a directory stops at a cut and misses the team's earlier commits. Use `git log --follow` on a file, or compare contents.
- To find who wrote something, or where the repository's history after 2012 comes from, read `research/authorship.md` and `explorations/coordinator/lineage.md`.
- Commit `8fe1daa8f` copied a third-party port of the tree to Java 9 onto the team's last commit, `a874948ac`. Give its lines no credit, and name no author of it in any text that you commit. In a reconstruction of authorship, attribute nothing of it to anyone.
# Exploring: a question that the record does not settle

The record keeps what earlier workers found, and they met many of the same questions. Workers have called a thing absent or new when the record already held it.

## The choices that are yours

The curator settles every conflict and every question about a decision of the curator. Any other choice is yours only if it meets all four of these conditions:

- It changes only one area.
- It changes no line of the model program.
- It changes no decision of the curator.
- It can be undone.

## Weighing the sources

The type group is the part of the team that built the type checker and the compiler, from 2009 to 2012. Where their late positions disagree with the specification's earlier text, the late positions weigh more. These positions are:

- the exclusion rule;
- compiled code specialised to each instantiation of a generic, which they kept;
- the compiled number tower, which they flattened in 2009 and 2010;
- the 2012 write-up on the Return Type Rule (`Papers/Types/journal/`);
- the POPL 2019 paper on symmetric multiple dispatch (`research/extracts/ParkPOPL2019-extract.md`).

The team's later work is outside the original tree. It is in these places:

- `research/extracts/`: the POPL 2019 paper, Steele's talks of 2015 and 2016, and the project's web sites with the post of July 2012 that ended the project;
- the reading of the team's 2012 patents: `explorations/reviews/mie-probes/patents-forest-rule.md`.

If a conflict or a decision not taken needs the designers' reason for a rule, print the row of its design area. WORD is a word of the area, such as `coercion`, `juxtaposition`, `dispatch` or `Arrays`. A word can match several rows, each about 1 to 2 KB.

    explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'map:design-intent-sources.md#The map, by design area@WORD'

Then open the sources that the row names. Among them are the `\note{}` boxes and the team's written rationale in the Internal Document appendix: `Specification/appendices/FAQ.tex` and `future.tex`. The row also names the later works that speak to its area, after the words "after the repository (§7)". To read what one of them covers and does not cover, print its row of the map's section "After the repository". WORD is a word of its title, such as `Polymorphic`, `patents`, `JuliaCon` or `Wrapping`. A row is about 1 to 2 KB.

    explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'map:design-intent-sources.md#After the repository@WORD'

When your report describes the team's sources on a question, say which of them is one of the late positions above. If the question is about a type rule, also name each later work that you checked.

## The procedure

1. Search the record with the queries in `records.md`. If two of the team's sources disagree, look for the construct in `revival-changes.md` before you search the record.
2. If the record or `revival-changes.md` settles the question, go back to building. Cite what settles it.
3. If you have evidence against a decision of the curator, read its POSITIONS entry and the notes that it names. If the decision used your evidence, go back to building.
4. Search the original tree. These help: the feature table and the phase map (`compiler.md`, "Before an edit"), the `\note{}` boxes and the map of design areas ("Weighing the sources" above), and the history of a file (`records.md`, "The repository's history").
5. Before you write that something does not exist, search the record for it, INDEX included (`index:WORDS`).
6. Decide whose choice it is, by "The choices that are yours" above.
7. Record each defect that you found as `tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded", says. If you make the choice and repair the defect, that is its item 1. If the question stays open, it is its item 3. Record a finding that is not a defect, such as a fact about the original tree, as `records.md`, "Writing to the record", says.
8. If your brief does not let you edit the ledger, put the ledger row in your report:
   1. Write the row in a file, in the form that `records.md` gives for a new row.
   2. Run `python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py check --rows FILE`. It counts the `?` in the number cell as a broken rule. Correct the row until the check names no other rule.
   3. Copy the row into your report.
9. If the question touches a passage of the specification, do as `specification.md`, "When the text and an implementation disagree", says.
10. If the choice is yours, make it. Report it as a decision.
11. If the choice is the curator's, report it as a decision not taken. Give these:
    - the question;
    - each source, and its date ("Weighing the sources" above says what else to note);
    - each possible solution, and what it changes;
    - which solution keeps the current behaviour.
12. If you cannot get some evidence in your task, say in your report what is missing and how to get it.
# Committing and pushing

**scratch**
: Files and folders that your work makes and `main` does not keep: logs, captured and raw run output, copies of tools, probe programs, lists and private caches folders.

Your brief says whether you commit and push, and on which branch. If it says nothing, commit on your current branch, and push it.

## What to commit

- Commit your change, its tests, your report if it is a file, and any reusable script.
- Commit what you write to the record, such as a ledger row, with the work that it records. A row's close follows the fix's commit (`records.md`).
- Keep scratch in your tree's `tmp/`, which is gitignored.
- In a fresh clone, `.claude/worktrees/` and `.claude/agents/` show as untracked, because the lines of `.git/info/exclude` that hide them are not in the clone. Do not commit them.
- Keep a copyrighted PDF or deck in `research/decks/`, which is gitignored. Cite it by its Wayback URL. Notes on it go in `research/extracts/`: your own summary, with brief attributed quotations.
- Put provenance and rationale in commit messages and reports, not in source comments.
- Name a model by its tier (Opus, Sonnet, Fable) in any text that you commit, commit messages included. Never write its model identifier, the API's name for the model, which starts with `claude-`.

## How to commit

Commit as you go, each commit in one command that names its paths:

    git add -- <paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <paths>

- The command commits only the paths that it names. Other agents may have uncommitted edits in your tree. Leave them alone.
- If you renamed a file with `git mv`, name its old path in `git commit` only, because `git add` refuses a path that no longer exists: `git add -- <new paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <new paths> <old paths>`.
- Never commit a copied directory, and never use `git add -A`.
- Before you commit more than a few hundred lines, stage them and read what you staged: `git add -- <paths> && git diff --cached --stat -- <paths>`.
- If the commit edits the original tree, say so in its message.
- End every commit message with this footer, exactly, whatever footer Claude Code suggests:

      Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
      Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01AmiXNpJxQ6TBwec4vJZHDB

  If your brief gives another session line, use it.

## Pushing

Push after every commit, so that a lost container loses nothing.

- If you work on your own branch, push it: `git push -u origin <branch>` the first time, then `git push`. Your brief says how the branch reaches `main`.
- If you work on `main`, other agents commit to it too. Push only your own commits:
  1. Run `git log origin/main..main`. Your commits are those whose hashes your own `git commit` printed.
  2. If it lists another agent's commit, run the command again shortly: that agent pushes right after it commits. If the commit stays, push nothing, and say so in your report.
  3. If it lists only your commits, push three times, in this order:

         git push origin main
         git push origin main:claude/worker-brief-fable-vnnuv8
         git push origin main:blinded-fable

     The third push keeps `blinded-fable` current. If the container is lost, the platform rebuilds it from that branch.
- Push no branch that this section does not name, unless your brief names it.
- If a push is refused, push nothing more, and say so in your report.

# What the revival changed in the team's Fortress

This part gives the departures of revived Fortress from the team's Fortress, and from what you expect from Java, Scala, Haskell or Julia. The team left three forms that disagree: the specification, walk with the interpreter's library, and the compiled path with the compiler's library. The rules below resolve them. Read the part whole, after `SKILL.md`, before work.

Each bold rule states the rule of this tree. A sentence that names a POSITIONS entry (P-N) states a decision of the curator. Build on a sentence without one, but do not cite it as a decision. Question a rule only on new evidence (`SKILL.md`, "When to explore"). Most rules follow the team's later type papers (`Papers/`) over the specification's early text (P-26; `exploring.md`). The Working Draft is the unrevised specification, in `Specification-1.0-frozen/`. Where a rule changed the specification, Appendix I keeps the original text (`specification.md`).

A sentence that cites a ledger row states a known departure of one path from a bold rule. A fix can change it, so do not assert it as correct in a test. A sentence that opens "Until the switch-over" states a limit of the compiler's library. The limit ends when the compiled path moves onto the interpreter's library, so do not fix it in the compiler's prelude (`compiler.md`). If a change is not here, search FACTS and POSITIONS (`records.md`) before you call a disagreement a conflict. An old note, a team test and your training can be right about the team's walk and wrong here: the number types do not nest, fixed-width arithmetic does not wrap, and walk converts arguments.

## Dispatch and overloading

**Overloads may differ in their static parameters (P-45).** An example is `ident[\T extends Shape\](x: T): T` beside `ident[\T extends Round\](x: T): T`. The Working Draft forbids such pairs. A declaration's declared domain is the set of argument types that its declared parameter types accept at some instance within its bounds: every `Shape` for the first `ident`. The checker applies the overloading rules of `SKILL.md` to declared domains. The more specific declaration's return type must be a subtype of the other's at every instance, not at one only.

**Where a declaration has static parameters, exclusion is read over the whole tuple of parameter types (P-152).** By the exclusion rule, a value of both domains has one instance of each generic type at each position, so those instances' static arguments are equal. The domains exclude where these equalities cannot hold together, or where some position excludes at the instance that they force. So `o[\T\](x: P[\T\], b: Box[\T\])` beside `o[\T\](x: Q[\T\], b: Box[\T\])`, with `P[\T\] excludes { Q[\T\] }`, is valid. Both paths refuse a pair where the equalities leave a static parameter free, as `o[\T, U\](x: Q[\U\], b: Box[\T\])` beside the first `o`: nothing ties `U` to `T`. In its test of whether two domains exclude each other, the checker puts the meet of a static parameter's declared bounds in the parameter's place where the parameter is a whole parameter type, an element of a tuple or a member of an intersection or union (P-157). Inside a static argument, as `T` in `Box[\T\]`, the parameter stays.

**Walk chooses by declared parameter types, never by the order of the declarations.** It compares declared domains where one lies strictly inside the other. Otherwise it compares the instances that the call makes. It infers a dotted generic method's static arguments from the arguments' run-time types, as for a generic function. A trait's generic method called with an argument outside a bound fails with "Cannot unify".

**Walk's load check is not the verdict of these rules.** It refuses some valid pairs and loads some invalid ones, and the checker differs from it on others. Before you change code to pass walk's check, or take its acceptance as proof, find the case in `interpreter.md`, "What walk checks": a case that cites a ledger row is a departure of walk. For example, walk compares two functional methods of a generic trait or object on their declared domains only at a call (row 780).

**Two functional methods with equivalent parameter types are duplicates, wherever `self` stands.** So the checker refuses `f(self, y: S)` beside `f(x: S, self)` in a trait `S`. Abstract declarations count:

- both paths refuse an abstract and a concrete method with the same parameter types in one trait;
- both paths refuse an object that inherits an abstract functional method from one trait and its body from another, unless the object declares the method itself (P-149). The Scala language accepts it.

The Meet Rule asks for a declaration that covers the meet of two overloads that neither exclude each other nor nest (`SKILL.md`, "Fortress as a language"). An abstract functional method also counts for it. So the checker refuses `h(self): ZZ32` in a trait `S` beside a top-level `h(x: String): ZZ32`: nothing covers the meet of `S` and `String`.

## Traits and objects

**The compiled checker applies the exclusion rule (P-43, P-97).** It refuses a type that extends two instantiations of one generic trait. Walk applies no instantiation exclusion, so it runs such a type and refuses overloads on two instantiations, as at `Tg[\3\]` and `Tg[\4\]` (row 416). The specification marks the Working Draft's examples that break the rule "Not allowed": do not copy them.

**A `comprises` clause speaks of values (P-60).** Every value of the trait that declares it is a value of a listed type. So a generic trait need not be listed if every type below it is below a listed type, as `Integral[\I\]` below `AnyIntegral`. A Java `permits` list names each direct subtype; this clause need not. Read so, several declarations can together cover the meet of two overloads. At load, walk checks extenders only against the clauses of the program's main component (row 551).

**`override` widens.** An `override` overrides an inherited declaration only where the inherited parameter types are strictly narrower than its own. To replace an inherited declaration at its own parameter types, declare it again without `override`. An `override` in a trait also overrides in every type below it. The checker checks that an overriding return type is a subtype. Walk refuses at load an `override` that, by this rule, overrides nothing, so a Java-style `override` in the library stops every program. Two departures: the checker accepts such an `override` (row 653), and the code generator refuses every `override` modifier (row 650).

**An object defines an inherited abstract method by bodies that together cover its parameter types (P-147).** It needs one body at those types, or several narrower bodies that cover them, with `comprises` clauses read. Walk refuses at load an object without static parameters that leaves one uncovered. Walk skips this check for a generic object (row 665). Walk stops its search for a cover at limits that `interpreter.md` gives, and the checker at the same limits. The checker refuses a cover by several bodies where the abstract or a covering method has static parameters (row 725).

**In a self-typed trait the checker types `self` as the trait met with the implementing type.** A trait `T` is self-typed if both conditions hold:

- `T` has no `comprises` clause, or one that lists only `...`;
- `T` has a parameter `X` bounded by `T` itself, as `trait T[\X extends T[\X\]\]` (P-146), or by a self-typed trait that `T` extends at `X`.

In `T`'s bodies, `self` has the intersection type of `T[\X\]` and `X`. So `floor(self): I = self` in `Integral[\I extends Integral[\I\]\]` is valid without a cast. The checker refuses a type that extends `T[\A\]` and is not an `A`. A compiled body of `T` that returns `self` fails the JVM's verification when its class loads (row 695).

When the checker applies the overloading rules to a method of `T`, `self` has the type `T[\X\]`, except in its test of whether two domains exclude each other. There `self` has the intersection type of `T[\X\]` and `X` (P-157). With this reading and the bounds that the test reads ("Dispatch and overloading"), the library's generic `+` and `-` between an array and a number are valid beside `AdditiveGroup`'s own. Walk loads the library's pairs, but refuses such a pair where a program's own component declares both (row 804).

**An indexed type's index parameter is bounded by `Index` (P-156).** An indexed type is a type whose values `a[i]` subscripts, such as an array. Its index parameter is the static parameter that gives the type of `i`. In the library, and in your own generic over such a type, write `I extends Index`. Walk runs the code without the bound. The checker refuses it when it checks against the interpreter's library, as the count stage does (`compiler.md`). Of the integer types, only `ZZ32` extends `Index`, and `Range` excludes `Index`. To the checker a numeral is an `IntLiteral`, which is no `Index`. So it refuses `f(3)` for `f(x: Index)`. Walk takes it (row 364). Pass a `ZZ32` value there instead. `a[3]` stays valid, because an array indexed by `ZZ32` takes a `ZZ32`. The Working Draft lets no trait type hold a tuple, but here a tuple whose element types are all `Index` types is an `Index`. So `m[i, j]` passes the pair `(i, j)` as one index. `Index` extends only `Any`, so such a tuple is still no `Object`. The empty tuple `()` is no `Index`. A function over `Index` and one over a tuple of `Index` types do not exclude each other. Until the switch-over, the compiler's prelude declares no `Index`, so a program that names it does not compile. Two departures:

- the checker refuses a tuple expression at a parameter of type `Index`, but takes one at a parameter of type `I`, where `I extends Index` (row 805);
- walk loads a function over `Index` beside one over a pair whose element types neither lie below `Index` nor exclude it (row 806).

**Pairs and triples are ordered only where each element type extends `StandardPartialOrder`.** This holds for `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` and `CMP`. Walk refuses another element type at the call, also where earlier elements decide, as `(1,()) < (2,())`. It also refuses numbers of two run-time types at one position, as `(1,2) < (1,2.5)` (row 511). Unordered deciding elements give `false`, or `Unordered` for `CMP`. The checker orders a `List[\E\]` only where `E extends StandardTotalOrder[\E\]`, so a list of `RR64` has no order there (P-154). Walk orders every list (row 774). A list's `=` stays element by element.

## Static parameters, `where` clauses and sizes

**A type parameter that a call does not fix takes its bound, not Scala's `Nothing` (P-48).** The checker takes the intersection of its upper bounds, narrowed by the expected type. Under walk, a parameter whose bound names itself stays open, printed `OPEN`, as in `BoxU[\OPEN\]`. Every value passes `OPEN` itself. Where walk compares overloads, a type that holds `OPEN` admits only what it admits at `Bottom`: beside `pick(x: Any)`, `pick(x: (T,T))` takes no `(1, 2)`. Walk still gives `Bottom` to these parameters:

- one with two bounds, neither below the other (row 591);
- one that an argument bounds only from above, with a bound that names another static parameter (row 612);
- one that only the result of a function expression without a return type fixes (row 587).

**Only the checker gives a call written as an argument the enclosing call's context (P-51).** If the enclosing call fails as written, the checker types the inner call again against each declaration's parameter type. So `takesBox64(mk())` compiles for `mk[\T\](): BoxT[\T\]`. Walk gives an argument no expected type, so there `mk()` takes its bound (row 705). Under walk, write `mk[\ZZ64\]()`.

**Three `where` forms are built (P-151).** Conditional extension is an `extends` entry with a `where` clause that binds no variable and states only constraints `T extends SomeTrait`. The type extends the parent only where they hold, as `List[\E\]` extends `LexicographicOrder[\List[\E\],E\] where { E extends StandardTotalOrder[\E\] }`. The other two forms:

- a condition of a function or method on its own static parameters, or of a method on its trait's, checked at a call;
- a type variable of a `where` clause in a `comprises` clause, as `AnyList comprises List[\E\] where [\E\]`.

The checker reads an `extends` entry with any other `where` clause as unconditional, without a message. Walk and the compiled run time apply a conditional extension at every instance (row 774). Walk runs a dotted call that breaks a method's condition (row 777). The code generator refuses a declaration with a `where` clause of its own (row 701). `compiler.md` gives the checker's gaps.

**Sizes are compared by their written form (P-55).** The checker checks sizes against their kind, and the run time carries each as a descriptor. Two sizes are equal when they are written alike after numeral arithmetic: `2 3` is `6`, but `s0 s1` is not `s1 s0`. A static parameter is not known to differ from a numeral, so in `typecase N[\b0\] of N[\0\] => ...` the arm is reachable. The checker refuses a size power above the exponent 4096, except of 0, 1 or -1. Walk refuses a negative exponent. The class loader computes a size without checking its kind, and stops on a negative exponent with a Java exception (row 675).

**A size known only at run time comes from `reflect` in `NatReflect.fsi`.** Its value, a `NatParam`, passed where the object type `N[\n\]` is expected, binds `n` at the call. Such a call runs compiled only after the switch-over.

## Numbers

**The number types are flat siblings (P-43).** The record calls this choice route A. Route C is the way not chosen: a checker rule under which the number types could nest again. The record still calls the number and order traits "the tower". That word does not mean that they nest.

**Under walk a numeral has a run-time class.** The checker types an integer numeral as `IntLiteral`, a sibling under `Number` that converts to the integer types, `QQ` and `RR64` (P-76). Walk gives a numeral the class `Int`, `Long` or `BigNum` by its value. These classes stand for `ZZ32`, `ZZ64` and `ZZ`, but a generic instantiates at the class: `Box[\Int\]` is not `Box[\ZZ32\]` (row 364). Walk answers `IntLiteral`'s arithmetic as a `ZZ32` (row 578). The library's factories `array1` and `array2` give a `Vector` or `Matrix` only at the eight number types, not at a user subtype of `Number`. Elsewhere they give a plain array, whose `+` and unary `-` fail dispatch under walk. Under walk, an inferred element type is a run-time class, so they give a plain array (row 721). Write the static argument.

**Arguments convert by declared coercions, and a generic call promotes.** Walk converts at a call, a typed binding and an assignment, and chooses the coercion by the run-time value; the checker chooses it statically (P-59). Promotion instantiates a generic declaration at the narrowest type into which all its arguments coerce (P-74). So `f[\T\](a: T, b: T)` on a `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64` runs at `ZZ64`. Walk does not promote the elements of a tuple or varargs: it takes their join (rows 395, 511). Where several declarations apply only by coercion and none is more specific, both paths stop: "Ambiguous coercion". Where the tied declarations differ only where the call passes a numeral, the checker reads the numeral as `ZZ32`, or `ZZ64` or `ZZ` where the value does not fit.

**An integer power answers its base's type (P-153).** In the interpreter's library, `^` takes an exponent of any integer type. At a negative exponent, 1 and -1 give their power, 0 raises `DivisionByZero`, and other bases raise `IntegerOverflow`. For a result that is not an integer, write `2.0^(-1)`, or a `QQ` base as `(2/3)^(-1)`, not `10^(-k)`. Until the switch-over, the compiler's library has integer powers only at `ZZ32`, `NN32` and `NN64`, each with an exponent of its own type; its `RR64` power takes an `RR64` or a `ZZ32` exponent, a negative one included. Its `ZZ32` power gives 0 at a negative exponent for other bases. At a base of 0 it throws a Java exception that no `catch` sees (rows 441, 523).

**`/` on two integers answers a `QQ`.** So `7 / 2` is `7/2`, not 3. Truncate with `DIV`, on both paths. `DIV` answers its operands' type and rounds toward zero. For a float, make one operand a float, as `(1.0 s) / n` for `ZZ32` values `s` and `n`. Convert each `ZZ64` operand with `asFloat`, as `asFloat(s) / asFloat(n)`. Until the switch-over, the compiler's library has no `QQ` and declares `/` only at `RR64`, so a compiled `7 / 2` is a static error.

## Reductions and comprehensions

A clause form is a reduction or comprehension with generators in brackets, as `SUM[j <- 0#n] f(j)`.

**A reduction's static argument depends on the path.** The checker does not infer it for `SUM`, `PROD`, `BIG MAX` and `BIG MIN`, whose bound names the parameter (row 731). Write it in every clause form, as `SUM[\ZZ32\][j <- 0#n] f(j)`. Other reductions take their bound, or the expected type where the bound does not fit. Walk instantiates a reduction at its value's declared type: a local variable's, or a top-level or local function's return type, also where the clause form ends a block. A method's return type, a field, a top-level variable, a parameter and an assignment do not direct it. Else walk takes the join of the elements' run-time types. If that join is outside the reduction's bound, each `+` runs at its operands' types. An element that does not convert to the instance stops in `__bigOperator`, "body param 1". Departures under walk:

- with no declared type, an empty `SUM` gives the integer 0 (row 716);
- a comprehension inside another clause form is built at its elements' run-time types (rows 20, 717);
- a written static argument that is not a number type ends an empty `SUM` in `CastError` (row 436).

**A reduction without an identity lifts its elements to `Maybe[\R\]` inside the reduction.** `BIG MIN`, `BIG MAX` and the string reduction `BIG //` extend `AssociativeReduction[\R\]`, whose `simpleJoin` takes and answers `R`. `BIG MAX` over a generator still answers `R`. Walk refuses at load a reduction without static parameters that declares `simpleJoin` at `Any` or untyped. A generic one stops at its first join. The team's tests do so: do not copy them.

## Implementation limits

**Walk has no static types until it runs the checker after the switch-over (P-12).** So walk runs programs that the checker refuses. Besides a `Boolean`, it takes a `Maybe` as an `if` condition, `Just` as true and `Nothing` as false. It refuses any other value. The specification and the checker take only a `Boolean`, so do not write a `Maybe` condition. The compiled path's own limits are in `compiler.md`.

**Write every parameter type.** The compiled path refuses a parameter without a type, of a function, a method or a local function: "Missing parameter type for". Walk runs it, except in a method that implements an abstract one (row 405). A component's function that leaves out its return type takes the api's declaration at its parameter types. With none or several, the checker types the body.

# The compiled checker, the code generator and the run time

**count stage**
: Script that runs the compiled checker over the interpreter's library, on the `FortressLibrary` component and the apis that it imports, and prints the errors in a table: `explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count/run.sh`. Its total is the checker count.

**distance stage**
: Stage of the gate that runs the compiled checker over fourteen components of the interpreter's library, `FortressLibrary` among them, runs each of the checker's steps on each component whatever the earlier steps report, and prints the errors in a table. Your brief gives its command when you need it.

The code of this area is in these directories:

- `scala_src/typechecker/`: the type checker, in Scala.
- `compiler/`: the disambiguator, the desugarers, overloading, `codegen/`, `NamingCzar` and `OverloadSet`.
- `runtimeSystem/`: `InstantiatingClassloader`, tasks and transactions.

The phases' names in the code are parse, PREDISAMBIGUATEDESUGAR, DISAMBIGUATE, GRAMMAR, PRETYPECHECKDESUGAR, INTEGERLITERALFOLDING, TYPECHECK, DESUGAR, OVERLOADREWRITE and CODEGEN.

## What the two paths share

After the phases, each path has its own code for these:

- Values: walk's `interpreter/evaluator/values/` (`FInt`, `FFloat`), and the compiled `compiler/runtimeValues/` (`FZZ32`, `FRR64`).
- Number natives: walk's glue classes, in `interpreter/glue/prim/` (`Int.java`, `Long.java`).
- Dispatch: walk searches at run time, in `OverloadedFunction`. The compiled path calls a dispatch method that `OverloadSet` generates.
- The run: `fortress run` starts a second JVM (`bin/run`), which never enters `Shell.java`.

Both paths run the helpers of `nativeHelpers/` (`simpleIntArith.java`) ("Natives").

The phases differ too: walk turns off some desugarings that the compiled path runs (`interpreter.md`, "Where a fix of walk belongs"). A fix of one of those desugarers changes only the compiled path.

## The compiler's prelude, until the switch-over

The compiled path uses the compiler's own prelude: `LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss`, `Library/CompilerLibrary.fss` and `Library/CompilerAlgebra.fss`. `Library/CompilerSystem.fss` is the compiled path's `System`.

Do not add a declaration to the three prelude files: they are deleted at the switch-over. Their tests stay.

## What the compiled path cannot compile yet

For a construct that it cannot compile yet, the code generator calls `sayWhat` or throws another `CompilerError`. Such a call or throw is a code-generator wall. The code generator has no case for these constructs:

- `label` and `exit`, `spawn`, and `atomic` used as an expression;
- a local function declaration, and an object expression;
- an array literal, such as `[1 2 3]`.

It also refuses a function, method, object or trait declaration with a `where` clause of its own, and a function or method with a contract (`requires`, `ensures`, `invariant`). It compiles a declaration whose `extends` entry has a `where` clause. The disambiguator, which both paths run, drops a trait's or object's contract, so the code generator never sees one, and walk does not check one either (ledger row 781). It refuses a function or method with a modifier other than `getter`, `setter`, `io`, `private` and `abstract`, such as `override` (ledger row 650).

The compiler's prelude has no array types, only `ZZ32Vector` and `StringVector`. Its `for` loops, comprehensions and reductions work over `ZZ32` ranges only. Its reductions give a `ZZ32` or a `String`.

Until the switch-over, a compiled test uses none of these. If a test needs one, write it as an `XXX` test that names the wall (`tests-writing.md`).

## What the code generator does

`SKILL.md`, "The compiled run time", gives the jars, the dispatch methods, the templates and the boxed numbers.

- It emits no primitive `double` arithmetic.
- The class loader rewrites a template's bytes with ASM. The emitted classfiles stay at version 1.6, because this rewriting keeps no stack-map frames. Do not raise the version.
- The `value` modifier has no effect on the representation.
- An array of `RR64` values is to be stored as an unboxed `double[]`. The code generator does not build it yet (`SKILL.md`, "The compiled run time"). If your task touches how arrays are stored, print the two POSITIONS entries on arrays first (about 2 KB):

      explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'positions:array is stored as' 'positions:array design'

## The run time

- The class loader is `runtimeSystem/InstantiatingClassloader.java`. The revival has changed it for sizes and for the lock on a class's first load (ledger row 417). Before you investigate a failure while a class loads, read ledger rows 408 and 559, which name it (`records.md`, "Reading the record").
- The compiled code keeps each mutable variable in a cell (`compiler/runtimeValues/MutableFValue.java`). Before each read and write of the cell, the generated code asks `BaseTask.inATransaction()` (`runtimeSystem/`). Inside an `atomic` block, the access goes through the transaction. So the transaction tracks the variables that the block touches.

## Natives

`import java com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.{...}` in a `.fss` file binds static Java methods over plain Java values.

A body `builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.Class.method")` binds one such method, a helper, too. At the parse, the compiled path, and not walk, rewrites the body as a call of the method through a generated `import java`, with `self` first in a trait or object (`compiler/BuiltinPrimitiveRewriter.java`). The checker then checks the declaration against the method's Java signature. In a compile, it reads `int` as `ZZ32`, `long` as `ZZ64`, `float` as `RR32`, `double` as `RR64`, `boolean` as `Boolean`, `String` as `JavaString`, `BigInteger` as `ZZ` and `Object` as `Any` (`NamingCzar.fortressTypeForForeignJavaType`). Walk calls the same method by reflection (`interpreter.md`, "Natives"). The compile stops in these cases:

- If the string is in that package but names no public static method: 'builtinPrimitive names no static helper: …'.
- If the string names a glue class or anything else outside that package: 'Variable builtinPrimitive is not defined.'
- If the declaration has a varargs parameter: the same message (ledger row 849).

To test a helper on the compiled path, write a compiled test whose own declarations bind it, as `compiler_tests/NativeHelperBindingCompiled.fss` does. Until the switch-over, a compiled test cannot reach the interpreter's library's bindings.

The count stage and the distance stage check the interpreter's library with the same rewrite. There, the checker differs from a compile in these ways:

- A string that names a glue class, or a declaration with a varargs parameter, does not stop the check. The body stays a call of `builtinPrimitive`, typed at the declared result type, and no Java signature checks it (ledger row 849).
- The checker reads a helper's Java types as the interpreter's library's types: `String` as `String`, not `JavaString`, and the rest as in a compile.
- A component that imports a DSL grammar is parsed by other code (`GraphRepository.syntaxExpand`), which does not rewrite its bindings. So, as for a glue class, no Java signature checks them.
- The count stage checks only the `FortressLibrary` component's bindings. A binding of another component, as `FortressBuiltin`'s, only the distance stage checks.

The checker, in a compile and in both stages, reads `int` as `NN32` or `Char`, and `long` as `NN64`, only for six helpers with fixed names (`NamingCzar.java:373-384`, `:494-503`). Examples are `makeNN32FromZZ32WithSpecialCompilerHackForNN32ResultType` for a result and `makeZZ32FromNN32WithSpecialCompilerHackForNN32ArgumentType` for a parameter. So a binding over `NN32`, `NN64` or `Char` that names any other helper is a type error for the checker. Walk loads it, because it carries these types in `int` and `long`.

The wrapper generator wraps every method of a class that it is given, the private methods too. If a type has no Fortress counterpart, it fails the whole import. So give every method of a helper class a signature that maps to Fortress, also a private method.

## Traps of the compiled path

- The compiler's prelude declares `print`, `println` and `String`'s `||` at `Object`, not `Any` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fsi:37`, `:55`, `:61`). So until the switch-over, the checker refuses a generic that prints a value of a type parameter written without a bound, or concatenates it onto a `String`. The message names `Object`, as 'Object->() is not applicable to an argument of type T.' does for `println`. In such a generic of a compiled program or test, write `T extends Object`. The generic then takes no tuple, function or `()`. The one library declares these operations at `Any` or `String`, so do not change its text for this limit.
- An api and the component that implements it must have the same name. The linker looks for a component with the api's own name. If there is none, the link fails ("Could not find an implementation for API"), and the run dies with `NoClassDefFoundError`.
- The compiled dispatch ignores the contravariance of a parameter of arrow type. The property `fortress.disable.contravariance` is true by default, so `OverloadSet` passes no variance. The team turned it off in 2012 (`c35aac139`). If a compiled call with function arguments picks another declaration than walk does, look here first.
- A clean link does not prove that every call has its method. Two calls die at run time with `NoSuchMethodError`:
  - a call of a functional method of an object that a trait's `comprises` clause lists, on a value whose static type is the object. An example is `num(R)`, where `trait Q comprises { R }` declares `abstract num(self): ZZ32` and `object R extends Q` gives its body. Call it through a value typed as the trait, as `q: Q = R` and then `num(q)` (ledger row 815);
  - a read of an exported object's value parameter, from a component that imports the api, where the exporting component names the parameter otherwise than the api. A value parameter is a parameter of the object's constructor, and also a field. An example is `Np(3).a`, where the api declares `object Np(a: ZZ32)` and the component `object Np(z: ZZ32)`. The export check compares no value parameter's name. Give each value parameter the api's name (ledger row 839).

## The checker's gaps

`revival-changes.md` gives the rules. This section gives where the checker applies them, and where it does not yet.

- Overloads: in its test of whether two domains exclude each other, the checker puts the meet of a static parameter's declared bounds in the parameter's place where the parameter is a whole parameter type, an element of a tuple or a member of an intersection or union (P-157). Inside a static argument, as `T` in `Box[\T\]`, the parameter stays. The paths differ on `tint[\T extends Red\](x: Box[\T\])` beside `tint[\T extends Blue\](x: Box[\T\])`, where `Red`, `Blue` and `Box` are objects. The checker refuses it, because `Box[\Bottom\]` lies in both domains, and walk loads it. No decision says which is right. Assert neither path's answer in a test (ledger row 786).
- A `where` clause's constraint: the checker checks a function's or functional method's constraint on its own static parameters at the call. At a dotted call, a candidate is not applicable where the receiver's static argument breaks the method's constraint. A trait's or object's own constraint is checked where its type is used, also at a constructor call; only the checker reads it, and the code generator refuses such a declaration (ledger row 701). A `where`-clause variable is a static parameter of the function's arrow type, inferred at the call. The checker does not yet check these, and no ledger row holds the first two:
  - at a dotted call, a constraint whose bound names the method's own static parameters or a `where`-clause variable;
  - at a type's use, a constraint whose bound names a `where`-clause variable;
  - a static argument written at a top-level call, against its parameter's bound (ledger row 470).
- Imports: `import A.{...}`, with the three dots written, imports every name of `A`. The overloading check also reads `A`'s declarations of a name that the component imports by name from another api. So `import A.{...}` beside `import B.{ pick }`, where both apis declare `pick(x: P)`, is refused: 'There are multiple declarations of pick' (ledger row 813). Leave the name out of the whole import, as `import A.{...} except { pick }`.
- An `except` clause leaves out each identifier that it lists, on both paths. The compiled path does not leave out an infix operator that it lists. So where a component lists `-` in `except` and declares its own `-` at the api's parameter types, the code generator stops. Walk runs the component's own `-` (ledger row 814).
- Conditional extension: the condition holds while the checker checks the `extends` entry itself, an object's value parameters and every member. It does not hold for the other `extends` entries, the static parameters, the declaration's own `where` clause, and the `excludes` and `comprises` clauses. The checker lets a member that it checked under the condition be called where the condition fails (ledger row 773).
- A `comprises` clause that lists a type at a `where`-clause variable, as `NatParam comprises { N[\n\] } where [\ nat n \]` or `AnyList comprises List[\E\] where [\E\]`: at a call, the checker gives the variable a fresh size or type, equal only to itself. Two values passed in one call get two. A fresh type is bounded by the binding and by the clause's constraints. The variable is in scope in the trait, except in its `extends` and `excludes` clauses. The checker gives no fresh type where it meets the trait as a supertype of another type. A program that declares such a trait does not compile: the code generator refuses the trait's `where` clause (ledger row 701). Where a generic type that the clause lists, as `List[\E\]`, gives the body of a member of the trait, the code generator crashes before it refuses the clause: 'E is not in the kind env' (ledger row 812). Departures: a fresh type also under a function type's result (ledger row 751), none for an extender that the clause does not list (ledger row 752), and a crash at a call, from outside the trait, of a member whose type names the variable (ledger row 756).

## The `fortress` commands

`Shell.java` dispatches `bin/fortress <command>`.

- To see what an early phase makes of a program, stop after that phase: `parse` (a syntax check), `disambiguate`, `grammar`, `desugar` or `typecheck`.
- `unparse` prints the syntax tree back as Fortress source. Use it to see what a desugaring made.
- `link` links a compiled component (the `link` step of a compiled `.test` file). `api` writes a component's api. `test` runs a program's `test` declarations under walk.
- The command chooses the library. Walk and `test` call `Shell.useInterpreterLibraries()`. Every other command calls `useCompilerLibraries()`. Each call points `WellKnownNames` and `Types` to its prelude, and sets the desugaring switches.

## Running

    cd ProjectFortress
    # after an ant compileAll that started the caches again: the library order (build-and-caches.md)
    ../bin/fortress compile <path>/P.fss
    ../bin/fortress run P [args]

A small program compiles in about 5 s and runs in about 1 s.

- A crash of the checker prints one line and hides the Java stack. To see the stack, put `-debug stacktrace` before the file: `../bin/fortress compile -debug stacktrace <path>/P.fss`.
- A failed compile of a program leaves a 0-byte jar in `bytecode_cache/`. A run of the program then prints "Could not load P" and "Resource not found". Read the compile's error instead: it gives the cause.

## Before an edit

Two notes under `explorations/coordinator/map/` help you find where a fix belongs. Both date from September 2026, so a status or a line number in them can be stale. Before you rely on a status, read the ledger rows that it cites. Before you rely on a line number, grep for the method's name.

- Before you add or fix a language feature, print its row of the feature table. WORD names the feature, such as `spawn`, `coercion` or `typecase`. A row is about 1 KB. It names the feature's section of the specification, its parser rule, checker class, walk site, code-generator site, prelude declaration and ledger rows.

      explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'map:spec-to-implementation.md#Feature by feature@WORD'

- If your edit is in one phase, and you need what runs before and after it on each path, print that phase's section. Name the section by its number and the first word of its title. A section is 1 to 3 KB. B.1 is the phase list, B.4 disambiguation, B.5 desugaring, B.6 type checking, B.7 overloading, B.10 the caches, B.11 the run time and B.12 the natives.

      explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'map:modules-and-phases.md#B.5 Desugaring'

- Before you change the text of a diagnostic, grep the `.test` files for it. A `.test` file can pin a whole diagnostic with `compile_err_equals`, its `file:line:column` included. `grep -l 'TEXT' ProjectFortress/*tests/*.test`, with words of the diagnostic as TEXT, lists the files that pin it. Update each of those in the same commit. A line that you add to or remove from a compiler test program moves the pinned spans below it.

## Testing an edit here

- For a quick loop on an edit of the checker or the code generator, compile the edited class into a scratch directory, and run the compiler with that directory first on its class path. This takes seconds, rebuilds nothing and changes nothing tracked. Give each run a fresh copy of the caches, because nothing checks the caches against the compiler that wrote them, and a compile of an unchanged program with a jar writes nothing:

      Q=$PWD/tmp/quick ; export FORTRESS_CACHES=$Q/caches ; CP=$(bin/fortress_classpath | tail -1)
      mkdir -p $Q/classes && javac -nowarn -cp "$CP" -d $Q/classes ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/<path>/X.java
      rm -rf $Q/caches && cp -a default_repository/caches $Q/caches
      java $JAVA_FLAGS -Dfile.encoding=UTF-8 -Dfortress.caches=$Q/caches -cp "$Q/classes:$CP" com.sun.fortress.Shell compile P.fss
      bin/fortress run P

  For a Scala file, compile it with `java -cp "$CP" scala.tools.nsc.Main -classpath "$CP" -d $Q/classes -encoding UTF-8 X.scala`. Then put the edit into the tree and build it for real.
- If your change is near transactions, top-level mutable state or the class loader's first load, do the four-thread atomic runs (`gate.md`).

## The checker's time

This section is for a change of the checker: its Scala under `scala_src/`, or `ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast` and the generators under `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/astgen/`, from which the build generates the checker's syntax tree and `Walker`.

The count stage takes `<out-file> <scratch>` and about 150 seconds, more under load. That is longer than the Bash tool's default time limit, so run it in the background (`session.md`). It writes a table to the out-file: the errors of each api, the total, the number of places with errors, and the first crash. It keeps the checker's whole output in `<scratch>/run.txt`, and its caches in `<scratch>`, so a run from the base build leaves the base build as it was.

The checker checks every api first, and the component only if no api has an error. In each api or component, it stops at the first of its stages that finds errors. The stages run in this order (`compiler/StaticChecker.java`, `checkCompilationUnit`):

1. The type hierarchy and the type check.
2. The overloading check, which also compares the overloads' return types.
3. In the component only, the export check (`library.md`, "Designing a change").

So the count misses the errors of the later stages, and a fix of an early error can raise it.

The table's rows tell a clean run from a run that the checker did not finish:

- `#total 0` and `#locations 0`: the checker reached the component and found no error.
- `#stopped`, in place of `#total` and `#locations`: the errors came from a phase before the checker, such as the parse. The checker reported none and did not reach the component. The script exits 1, and the gate reads the table as red.
- `#crash`: the first crash of the overloading check that the run survived, or `none`.

If the run printed no error total and was not clean, the script writes no table and exits 1.

The checker's results are the programs that it accepts and refuses, and each error with its text and its place. On the interpreter's library, a change keeps the results the same if both of these hold:

- The two tables are equal: `diff` prints nothing.
- The two `run.txt` files are equal after you replace each run's own tree path with one word, such as `TREE`. Any difference fails.

A node's hash starts from its class's name, so an order in the output, such as the apis' checks or a union's members, moves only where the change itself moves it. Such a move is a difference: keep the old order, or report the difference, as for any other.

`Walker`, in the generated `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/nodes/FortressAst.scala`, is split into methods under 8,000 bytes of bytecode. HotSpot does not compile a longer method, and the walker runs on every node, so one long walker method slows the whole checker. `MethodSizeJUTest` fails if a method of the build grows past the limit, except the methods that its source lists in `listed(...)` entries. Run it alone with `ant testOnly -DtestPattern=MethodSizeJUTest`. If a method of `Walker` fails, lower `WALKER_CASES_PER_METHOD` in `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/astgen/ScalaAstGenerator.java`. If another method fails, split it under the limit. List it only if nothing in the checker or a compiled run calls it, with its size and what runs it, and name it in your report.

The timing is a smoke test. It is there to catch a slowdown of several times, or of orders of magnitude: a change that makes the checker three times slower must show. One run of each tree is enough. A small difference, or one within the noise from run to run, is not a finding. In your report, say what you saw, and do not analyse it.

If you change the checker:

1. Make the change correct, with its tests. Commit it, and name the commit in your report.
2. Time the base build and the change, named `base` and `change`. Run the base in a call set up for the base build (`build-and-caches.md`), and the change in a call set up for your tree, each in the background (`session.md`). Use the same command for both, with `N` the run's name:

       export W=<your tree> N=base ; mkdir -p $W/tmp/count
       time explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count/run.sh $W/tmp/count/$N.txt $W/tmp/count/$N

3. Make a second pass that makes the checker faster. Start with a profile (below). Where the profile shows a gain, take it. Where it shows none, say so in your report, with the profile's top frames.
4. After the second pass, run the count stage once more with the command of step 2, named `pass`. Show that its results are the same as `change`'s. Then run `ant testQuick` once more (`tests-running.md`, "When to run a whole suite").
5. If the pass reuses an answer that the checker computed earlier, as a memo does, audit it on one full run. Put the audit in an instrumented copy ("Testing an edit here"), never in the tree. In the audit, compute each reused answer again and compare the two. If any answer differs, the reuse is wrong: fix it or drop it, then repeat step 4. Report the count of reuses and of differences.
6. In your report, give each run's seconds, the diff of the `base` and `change` tables, the comparison of their `run.txt` files, and that `pass` has the same results as `change`.

To find where the time goes, use JFR on the count stage's checker, instrumented copies compiled into a scratch folder ahead of the build on the class path, and the methods over 8,000 bytes that `MethodSizeJUTest` lists in its source. A profiled or instrumented run is neither a timed run nor a run to compare. Print the commands of two earlier speed probes (about 8 KB):

    explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/perf-probes/checker-speed-2/REPORT.md#Decisions, findings' 'doc:explorations/perf-probes/checker-speed/REPORT.md#Decisions, findings'

If your brief asks you to review a change of the checker, run the count stage yourself. Time the base build and the worker's commit of step 1 once each, as step 2 says, with the commit and the worker's head in worktrees seeded at them (`worktrees.md`). Check that your times are the worker's, in order of size. Check that the commit's and the head's results are the same.

# Polymorphic Symmetric Multiple Dispatch with Variance

Gyunghee Park (KAIST and Oracle Labs), Jaemin Hong (KAIST), Guy L. Steele Jr.
(Oracle Labs) and Sukyoung Ryu (KAIST), *Polymorphic Symmetric Multiple
Dispatch with Variance*, Proceedings of the ACM on Programming Languages 3,
POPL, Article 11, January 2019, 28 pages, doi:10.1145/3290324
(https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3290324). The paper was presented at POPL
2019.

## The files

- `3290324-popl19w.pdf`: the paper as ACM published it, 28 pages.
- `3290324-popl19-TR.pdf`: the technical report, *Polymorphic Symmetric
  Multiple Dispatch with Variance (Extended with Formalization)*, 74 pages.
  It is the paper extended with the formalization, in appendices on the
  conditional type relations, the type matching rules, the lemmas and the
  proofs of the theorems.

The report's LaTeX sources:

- `paper.tex`: the main file, with the title, the authors and the abstract.
  It reads `macros.tex`, then the chapters below in this order.
- `intro.tex` (Introduction), `motiv.tex` (Motivation), `lang.tex`
  (Language), `rules.tex` (Overloading Rules), `resolve.tex` (Overloading
  Resolution), `related.tex` (Related Work), `conclude.tex` (Conclusion) and
  `appendix.tex` (the appendices).
- `macros.tex`: the report's own macros.
- `ref.bib`: its bibliography.
- `fortify.sty`: Sukyoung Ryu's copy of `Fortify/fortify.sty`, the Fortress
  project's macros for typesetting Fortress code, with its Oracle copyright
  notice. It differs from the project's last version of that file in two
  places: it loads no `amssymb`, and it sets type names in `\mathtt`, not
  `\mathrm`.
- `bcprules.sty`: "BCP's latex tricks for typesetting inference rules",
  version 1.4, as its header names it.
- `metanotation.sty`: macros for the notation of the rules: boxed
  expressions, repetitions with separators and bindings, and don't-care
  marks.
- `acmart.cls`: ACM's article class, version 1.43 of 2017/07/09.
- `ACM-Reference-Format.bst`: ACM's bibliography style, version 2.1 of 14
  June 2017.

The technical report and its sources are included with Sukyoung Ryu's
permission. She permitted the report on 2026-10-29: "It's okay to include it
publicly in the repository." She sent the sources on 2026-10-30.

   239	\subsection{Well-formedness}\label{sec:wellformed}
   240	
   241	We define well-formedness of a program and its declarations as shown in
   242	Figure~\ref{fig:wellformed}.
   243	A type-declaration environment $\Delta$ is a set of class declarations and
   244	type parameter bindings, and
   245	a variable-type environment $\Gamma$ is a sequence of bindable variables
   246	and their types.  Checking well-formedness may introduce
   247	\textit{internal types}:
   248	\begin{center}
   249	$\descsm{Internal type} \quad \alpha~::= P~\mid~C~\mid~\tupleb{\alpha}~\mid~
   250	\arrowtype{\alpha}{\alpha}~\mid~\Any~\mid~\Bottom~\mid~
   251	\uniontype{\alpha}{\alpha}~\mid~\intersectiontype{\alpha}{\alpha}$
   252	\end{center}
   253	which contain $\Bottom$, union types, and intersection types.
   254	Type $\Bottom$ is a subtype of every type; hence, $\Any$ and $\Bottom$
   255	are the top and bottom, respectively, of the type lattice.
   256	Metavariables $\alpha, \gamma, \rho, \chi, \eta$ range over internal types.
   257	We introduce metavariables $K$, $C$, $J$, and $M$,
   258	analogous to $\kappa$, $c$, $t$, and $\mu$, respectively, where 
   259	types $\tau$ in the latter are replaced by internal types $\alpha$ in the former.
   260	
   261	Rule \rncite{T-Program} states that a program is well-formed
   262	if its class declarations have distinct names and are well-formed, and
   263	its top-level expression is well-formed.

   281	We compare domain types to decide whether one generic method
   282	declaration is more specific than the other;
   283	an existential type $\existstypebigb{K}{\alpha}$ is a subtype of another
   284	existential type $\existstypebigb{K'}{\alpha'}$ if there exists
   285	a well-formed substitution $\sigma$ for the type parameters bound in $\rep{K'}$ that makes
   286	$\sigma\alpha'$ a supertype of $\alpha$.
   287	A substitution is well-formed if it satisfies the bounds of type parameters
   288	as shown in Figure~\ref{fig:wellformedsubst}.
   289	In contrast, we compare arrow types to see whether the return type
   290	of a more specific generic method declaration can be a subtype of the return
   291	type of a less specific one;
   292	a universal type $\foralltypebigb{K}{\alpha}$ is a subtype of the other
   293	universal type $\foralltypebigb{K'}{\alpha'}$ if there exists
   294	a well-formed substitution $\sigma$ for the type parameters bound in $\rep{K}$ that
   295	makes $\sigma\alpha$ a subtype of $\alpha'$.
   296	Figure~\ref{fig:quantified} formally defines these ``inner'' subtyping
   297	rules for quantified types.  (We assume the usual conventions about
   298	using $\alpha$-conversion to rename bound variables when necessary
   299	to satisfy premises that require variable names to be distinct.)
   300	Finally, the intersection type of two
   301	existential types $\existstypebigb{K}{\alpha}$ and
   302	$\existstypebigb{K'}{\alpha'}$ used in [{\sc Meet-Excl}] and [{\sc Meet-Third}] is
   303	$\exists{\big\llbracket\verythinmathspace \bar{K},\bar{K'} \verythinmathspace\big\rrbracket}{\intersectiontype{\alpha}{\alpha'}}$,
   304	because whenever both $\sigma\alpha$ and $\sigma'\alpha'$ are supertypes
   305	of a type $\tau$ for some $\sigma$ and $\sigma'$,
   306	$(\sigma\compose\sigma')\intersectiontype{\alpha}{\alpha'}$ is a supertype of
   307	$\tau$ as well.
   308	
   309	While the subtype relation of domain types is a sound
   310	approximation of the subset relation of applicable sets, it is not
   311	complete; when the applicable set of one declaration is a subset
   312	of that of the other, their domain types may not be in a subtype relation.
   313	Consider the following:
   314	\[
   315	\begin{array}{l}
   316	m\ob{P}(x:{\sf ArrayList}\ob{P})\ \dontcare\andalso
   317	m\ob{Q\extends T}(y:{\sf List}\ob{Q})\ \dontcare\andalso
   318	m\ob{R\extends T}(z:{\sf ArrayList}\ob{R})\ \dontcare
   319	\end{array}
   320	\]
   321	for some trait $T$ where ${\sf ArrayList}$ extends ${\sf List}$ and both
   322	are invariant, and call them $d_1$, $d_2$, and $d_3$ in order.
   323	Even though they are a valid overloading because the applicable set of
   324	$d_3$ is the intersection of those of $d_1$ and $d_2$,
   325	the intersection of the two domain types
   326	$\Xi_{\sqcap}=\existstype{P,Q\extends T}{\intersectiontype{{\sf ArrayList}\ob{P}}{{\sf List}\ob{Q}}}$
   327	is not a subtype of the domain type of $d_3$, 
   328	$\Xi_3=\existstype{R\extends T}{{\sf ArrayList}\ob{R}}$.
   329	However, because ${\sf ArrayList}$ extends ${\sf List}$ and both are
   330	invariant, any subtypes of theirs are exclusive unless they are both
   331	${\sf ArrayList}\ob{S}$ for some type $S$ that is a subtype of $T$.
   332	Thus, $\Xi_{\sqcap}$ denotes the same applicable set as
   333	$\existstype{S\extends T}{{\sf ArrayList}\ob{S}}$, which is
   334	a subtype of $\Xi_3$ using $\subst{R}{S}$.
   335	
   336	
   337	Therefore, in order to reduce the gap between the subset relation of
   338	applicable sets and the subtype relation of domain types,
   339	we extend the subtype relation of existential types using
   340	\emph{existential reduction}.  As defined in Figure~\ref{fig:quantified},
   341	existential reduction infers a simplified existential type from a given
   342	existential type $\existstype{\rep{K}}{\alpha}$.
   343	As defined in Figure~\ref{fig:constraints}, it first collects
   344	constraints $\C$ that make $\alpha$ different from $\Bottom$:
   345	${\Delta}\turnstile{\alpha}\,{\not\equiv}\,{\Bottom}\Rightarrow{\C}$.
   346	It then tries to find types that instantiate the type parameters bound in
   347	$\rep{K}$ or simply collects their bounds by solving $\C$ and the
   348	constraints on the type parameters; it makes a substitution $\sigma$
   349	for the type parameters that have types to instantiate with and
   350	constraints $\C''$ for the type parameters that have only bounds.
   351	Using the substitution $\sigma$ and type parameter bindings $\rep{K'}$
   352	generated from $\C''$, it produces a simplified existential type
   353	$\existstype{\rep{K'}}{\sigma\alpha}$.  Finally, in the extended subtype
   354	relation, one existential type is a subtype of the other if a reduced
   355	existential type of the former is a subtype of the latter
   356	by the inner subtyping rule as shown in Figure~\ref{fig:quantified}.

   440	Collecting constraints $\C$ that make a type $\alpha$ different from
   441	another type $\alpha'$ requires various relations between types such as
   442	subtype, non-subtype, equivalence, non-equivalence, exclusion, and
   443	non-exclusion relations.  A constraint is inductively defined with

   445	non-subtype, exclusion, and non-exclusion relations as base cases,
   446	and conjunction and disjunction of constraints as inductive steps.
   447	We also defined the various type relations inductively on the structure
   448	of types.  In addition, we defined all the type relations in a way that
   449	supports complete and disjoint case analysis for types.  The entire type
   450	relations are formally defined in Appendix~\ref{app:condrel}.

   453	Arrow types are compared only in rule \rncite{Return-Test},
   454	to see whether the return type of a more specific
   455	generic method declaration can be a subtype of the return type of a less
   456	specific one.  As the informal rule in Section~\ref{sec:motiv:fgf}
   457	specifies, Return Type Rule checks that for two declarations
   458	$d_1$ and $d_2$ where $d_1$ is more specific than $d_2$, and
   459	for any non-$\Bottom$ type $\gamma$ that $d_1$ is applicable to,
   460	the return type of an instance of $d_2$ that is applicable to
   461	$\gamma$ is a supertype of the return type of some instance of
   462	$d_1$ that is applicable to $\gamma$.
   463	When the arrow types of $d_1$ and $d_2$ are
   464	$\foralltypeb{\kappa}{\arrowtype{\alpha}{\rho}}$ and
   465	$\foralltypeb{\kappa'}{\arrowtype{\alpha'}{\rho'}}$, respectively,
   466	\rncite{Return-Test} checks this by checking whether the arrow type of
   467	$d_1$ is a subtype of
   468	$\foralltype{\bar{\kappa},\bar{\kappa'}}{\arrowtype{\intersectiontype{\alpha}{\alpha'}}{\rho'}}$.
   469	Since $d_1$ is more specific than $d_2$ and is applicable to $\gamma$,
   470	there exist substitutions $\sigma_1$ and $\sigma_2$ that make $d_1$ and
   471	$d_2$ applicable to $\gamma$, respectively, thus both $\sigma_1\alpha$
   472	and $\sigma_2\alpha'$ are supertypes of $\gamma$, therefore so is
   473	$(\sigma_1\compose\sigma_2)\intersectiontype{\alpha}{\alpha'}$.
   474	Thus, if the arrow type of $d_1$ is a subtype of
   475	$\foralltype{\bar{\kappa},\bar{\kappa'}}{\arrowtype{\intersectiontype{\alpha}{\alpha'}}{\rho'}}$
   476	using some substitution $\sigma$, it makes $\sigma\alpha$ a supertype of
   477	$\intersectiontype{\alpha}{\alpha'}$, which makes
   478	$(\sigma_1\compose\sigma_2\compose\sigma)\alpha$ a supertype of $\gamma$,
   479	and $\sigma\rho$ a subtype of $\rho'$.
   480	Hence, $\sigma_1\compose\sigma_2\compose\sigma$ is the
   481	one that makes the instance of $d_1$ that is applicable to $\gamma$
   482	and has the return type that is a subtype of the instance of $d_2$.

   484	for any instance of $d_2$ instantiated with $\sigma_2$
   485	that is applicable to $\gamma$, there exists an instance of $d_1$
   486	instantiated with $\sigma_1\compose\sigma_2\compose\sigma$
   487	that is applicable to $\gamma$ and has a return type that is a subtype
   488	of the return type of the instance of $d_2$.

   346	The \textsf{match} rules in Figure~\ref{fig:match} compute lower and upper
   347	type bounds $\biglistofb{\listofb{\lbound}}$ and
   348	$\biglistofb{\listofb{\ubound}}$ for method type parameters in $\bar{K}$
   349	by matching a ground type $g$ against an internal type $\alpha$ according
   350	to a variance mark $V$.
   351	When $V$ is respectively $\bindco$, $\bindcontra$, or $\bindinv$, the rules compute 
   352	the type bounds that make $g$ respectively a subtype, a supertype, or an equivalent type of $\alpha$.
   353	For example, as in~\rncite{M-Param-Co}, if a ground type $g$ is
   354	matched against a method type parameter $P_i$ according to $\bindco$,
   355	$g$ becomes the lower bound of $P_i$ so that $g$ is a subtype of $P_i$
   356	as long as $P_i$ satisfies its type bounds $g \subtypeof P_i \subtypeof \Any$.
   357	
   358	The \textsf{match} rules compute lower and upper type bounds
   359	in the form of two lists of lists
   360	$\biglistofb{\listofb{\lbound}}$ and $\biglistofb{\listofb{\ubound}}$
   361	where $\countofb{\listofb{\lbound}} = \countofb{\listofb{\ubound}}$ and
   362	$\rep{\countofb{K} = \countofb{\lbound_i} = \countofb{\ubound_i}}[i]$.
   363	Matching may produce multiple solutions; each inner list is one possible solution.
   364	Multiple solutions come from cases with union types and
   365	intersection types as in rule~\rncite{M-Union-Whatever-Contra}, which
   366	matches a union ground type $\naryuniontypeb{g}$ against $\alpha$
   367	according to $\bindcontra$ and computes type bounds that make
   368	$\naryuniontypeb{g}$ a supertype of $\alpha$.  Because a union type
   369	$\naryuniontypeb{g}$ is a supertype of $\alpha$ if any component $g_i$
   370	is a supertype of $\alpha$, multiple components may be supertypes of
   371	$\alpha$, which may lead to multiple type bounds for each of those
   372	components.  Since we cannot decide which one of the multiple type bounds
   373	is the one eventually satisfying all the constraints, the \textsf{match}
   374	rules compute all possible solutions, which are then winnowed in the solving step.
   375	To collect all the bounds, the \textsf{match} rules cover failure
   376	cases as well so that the rules do not stop collecting bounds even
   377	when one component fails type matching.  For example,
   378	rule~\rncite{M-Tuple-Tuple-Failure} specifies a failure case due to
   379	size mismatch of tuple types; rather than actually failing,
   380	it succeeds but delivers empty lists of solutions.
