   484	The last step of the dispatch semipredicate is to solve the computed type
   485	bounds for method type parameters as in Figure~\ref{fig:solve}.
   486	The \textsf{solve} rules compute a valid substitution $\sigma$ for all the
   487	method type parameters in $\bar{K}$, which satisfies the declared
   488	bounds in ${\bar{K}}$ and the computed bounds from type matching
   489	$\biglistofb{\listofb{\lbound}}$ and $\biglistofb{\listofb{\ubound}}$.
   490	The solving step succeeds if any of the type bounds leads to a valid
   491	substitution.  For declared type bounds for method type parameters
   492	$\rep{P}, P'$ and their computed type bounds
   493	$\biglistofb{\listof{\rep\lbound,\lbound'}}$ and
   494	$\biglistofb{\listof{\rep\ubound,\ubound'}}$ from type matching,
   495	rule~\rncite{Solve-Step} nondeterministically selects $i$-th type bounds
   496	$\listof{\rep{\lbound_{\same{i}}}, \lbound'_i}$ and
   497	$\listof{\rep{\ubound_{\same{i}}}, \ubound'_i}$ that successfully compute
   498	a valid substitution.  Starting from the rightmost type parameter
   499	$P'$, the rule computes a substitution $\subst{g'}{P'}$ by taking the
   500	intersection of the upper bounds of $P'$.  Because $g'$ is a ground type,
   501	the solving step never instantiates method type parameters with $\Bottom$.
   502	The \textsf{match} premises propagate the choice of $g'$ for $P'$ to the
   503	declared lower bounds of $P'$ to collect additional constraints on
   504	$\rep{P}$.  Then, the rule combines the additional constraints and the
   505	originally computed bounds, and inductively solves the combined bounds
   506	to compute the substitution $\substb{g}{P}$.  From this, it produces a valid
   507	substitution $\substbx{g}{P}{g'}{P'}$.
   508	
   509	Note that the rule selects $i$-th type bounds nondeterministically while
   510	it checks type parameters deterministically from the rightmost one.
   511	Because the scope of a well-formed method type parameter extends to the
   512	right and method type parameters can appear only in lower bounds,
   513	for well-formed type parameters $\rep{\lobindup{\bar\chi}{P}{\bar\eta}}$,
   514	the upper bounds $\bar{\setb{\eta}}$ do not contain any of $\bar{P}$, and
   515	$P_j$ does not appear in the lower bounds of $P_i$ for $i\le j$.
   516	Thus, the choice of $g_i$ for $P_i$ does not affect the upper
   517	bounds of $P_j$, which allows us to compute a substitution in the
   518	right-to-left order by taking intersections of upper bounds.
   519	Since the choice of $g_j$ for $P_j$ may place additional constraints on
   520	$P_i$'s that appear in the lower bounds $\setb{\chi_{\same{j}}}$ of $P_j$,
   521	\rncite{Solve-Step} propagates the choice of $g_j$ for $P_j$ to the
   522	lower bounds and computes additional constraints, to ensure
   523	that $g_j$ is a supertype of all $\setb{\chi_{\same{j}}}$.

   527	Let us revisit the dynamic overloading resolution process with a concrete example.
   528	Suppose we have two covariant traits $\kwd{List}$ and $\kwd{SortedList}$

   530	two objects $\kwd{Cons}$ and $\kwd{SortedCons}$ such that
   531	$\kwd{Cons}\ob{P} \extends \kwd{List}\ob{P}$ and
   532	$\kwd{SortedCons}\ob{P} \extends \kwd{SortedList}\ob{P}$, and
   533	a method $\mathit{append}$ that concatenates two lists.

   672	\subsubsection{Correctness of Dispatch Semipredicate}\label{sec:prop}~\\
   673	We prove the soundness and completeness of the dispatch semipredicate
   674	by showing that each of its steps is sound and complete.
   675	
   676	We first show that the type matching step is sound and complete.
   677	
   678	The \textsf{match} rules compute sound bounds for method type parameters
   679	by matching a ground type $g$ against an internal type $\alpha$ according
   680	to a variance mark $V$.  That is, any substitution $\sigma$ satisfying
   681	the bounds makes $\sigma\alpha$ a supertype, a subtype, or an equivalent type of
   682	$g$ when $V$ is respectively $\bindco$, $\bindcontra$, or $\bindinv$.
   683	
   684	\begin{lemma}(Soundness of Type Matching)\\
   685	\label{lem:matchsound}
   686	Let $\rep{K=\lobindup{\rep{\chi}}{P}{\rep{\eta}}}$,
   687	$\jscope[\denv]{\obb{K}}$,
   688	$\jwftype[\denv]{g}$,

  1034	\subsection{Discussion}\label{sec:discuss}
  1035	Defining a provable system for an object-oriented language requires addressing
  1036	various technical challenges due to the structural asymmetries inherent
  1037	in the language design.  One can have a variable of type $\Any$,
  1038	but one cannot have a variable of type $\Bottom$.  The ilk of an actual
  1039	argument must be a subtype, not a supertype, of the method's parameter
  1040	type.  The ilk of a returned value must be a subtype, not a supertype, of
  1041	the method's return type.  A trait may declare ancestors but not
  1042	descendants.  Such asymmetries prohibit
  1043	seemingly symmetric features from being treated as duals.  One might think
  1044	at first glance that upper bounds and lower bounds of type parameters
  1045	should be related symmetrically (perhaps treated as duals), but they cannot be.
  1046	
  1047	For example, the ``Ancestor Meet Rule''
  1048	(expressed in this paper by rule \rncite{Anc-Same-Trait}) was introduced
  1049	into Fortress in 2012 by Guy Steele and David Chase~\cite{dchase12} to
  1050	design an expressive type system with union and intersection types.  This rule
  1051	permits proofs that (a)~if $T\ob{P}$ is covariant in $P$ then
  1052	$T\ob{\intersectiontype{\alpha}{\alpha'}}\equiv \intersectiontype{T\ob{\alpha}}{T\ob{\alpha'}}$, and
  1053	(b)~if $T\ob{P}$ is contravariant in $P$ then
  1054	$T\ob{\uniontype{\alpha}{\alpha'}}\equiv \intersectiontype{T\ob{\alpha}}{T\ob{\alpha'}}$
  1055	(that last set operator is indeed $\sqcap$, not $\sqcup$).
  1056	These equivalences allow simplification of type expressions by moving type union
  1057	and type intersection operators out of type arguments.
  1058	However, the ``obvious other two cases'' are not available.
  1059	When $T\ob{P}$ is covariant in $P$, $T\ob{\uniontype{\alpha}{\alpha'}}$
  1060	is not equivalent to some simple combination of $T\ob{\alpha}$ and $T\ob{\alpha'}$;
  1061	the best one can say is that $\uniontype{T\ob{\alpha}}{T\ob{\alpha'}} \subtypeof T\ob{\uniontype{\alpha}{\alpha'}}$.
  1062	
  1063	In 2012, the developers of Fortress explored an alternate set of language restrictions
  1064	that exploited these asymmetries to ensure that exponential blowup could occur at run time
  1065	only when union types interacted with contravariance (the dual case of intersection types
  1066	interacting with covariance could not occur).  They then
  1067	contemplated two alternatives for avoiding the exponential blowup.
  1068	One possibility is to eliminate contravariant type parameters and contravariant type relationships.
  1069	This has the consequence that arrow types must be treated as invariant, rather than contravariant,
  1070	in the type to the left of the arrow.
  1071	This could make it inconvenient to use higher-order functions such as
  1072	$\mathit{map}$, but one can compensate by introducing rules of
  1073	coercion, so that if a function of type $\arrowtype{\alpha}{\rho}$ is
  1074	used in a situation where a function of type $\arrowtype{\alpha'}{\rho'}$ is required,
  1075	it can be coerced to a new function object if $\alpha'\subtypeof\alpha$ and $\rho\subtypeof\rho'$.
  1076	The other possibility is to eliminate union types from the type
  1077	theory; this might require restricting the language so that, for
  1078	example, in an \texttt{if}-\texttt{then}-\texttt{else}
  1079	expression, the type of the $\texttt{then}$ subexpression must be
  1080	either a supertype or a subtype of the $\texttt{else}$ subexpression.
  1081	Alternatively, some sort of pseudo-join (least common existing supertype) operation could be used.
  1082	One could go even further, also eliminating intersection types from the type theory
  1083	by further restricting the language and possibly using a pseudo-meet operation.
  1084	
  1085	% In this paper, we carefully designed the dynamic dispatch algorithm to
  1086	% make a balanced tradeoff between static expressivity and dynamic
  1087	% efficiency.  We accept the potential for exponential blowup during
  1088	% dynamic dispatch because we believe that such cases are unlikely to
  1089	% arise in practice and the use of union and intersection types in the
  1090	% type theory, even if not directly expressible by the programmer, makes
  1091	% the language more expressive.  Also, while one could in principle
  1092	% allow any lower bound to refer to any type parameter, dynamic
  1093	% overloading resolution would then have to solve a general set of type
  1094	% inequalities, requiring a complex technique with multiple iterations;
  1095	% we chose instead to impose left-to-right scoping on method type
  1096	% parameters, so as to allow the use of a simple, one-pass right-to-left scan.
  1097	
  1098	We carefully designed our dynamic dispatch algorithm to
  1099	make a balanced tradeoff between static expressivity and dynamic
  1100	efficiency.  We accept the potential for exponential blowup
  1101	% during dynamic dispatch
  1102	because we believe that such cases are unlikely to
  1103	arise in practice and the use of union and intersection types in the
  1104	type theory, even if not directly expressible by the programmer, makes
  1105	the language more expressive.  Also, while one could in principle
  1106	allow any lower bound to refer to any type parameter, dynamic
  1107	overloading resolution would then have to solve a general set of type
  1108	inequalities, requiring a complex technique with multiple iterations;
  1109	we chose instead to impose left-to-right scoping on method type
  1110	parameters, allowing use of a simple, one-pass right-to-left scan.
  1111	We believe this tradeoff represents a relatively small sacrifice of expressivity for
  1112	a large gain in dynamic efficiency.
  1113	
  1114	Dynamically inferring type instantiations can incur run-time overhead.
  1115	In simple invariant cases, we expect the run-time cost to be relatively low but nonzero.
  1116	For example, if we pass a value of type \texttt{List$\ob{\texttt{String}}$} to a method such as
  1117	\textit{foo}$\ob{T}$\texttt{($x$:List$\ob{T}$)},
  1118	$T$ is matched only once and no union or intersection types are involved.
  1119	If \texttt{List} is invariant in $T$, it will come down to extracting the type \texttt{String}
  1120	from the type \texttt{List$\ob{\texttt{String}}$} and binding $T$ to that.
  1121	For more costly covariant and contravariant cases,
  1122	as in certain JVM implementations, such techniques as caching or dynamic recompilation
  1123	in reaction to the relative frequencies of types actually encountered may help.
  1124	
  1125	The biggest challenge we faced in trying to find a provable system was
  1126	grappling with the language asymmetries described above and trying to
  1127	understand their consequences.  In particular, the Fortress team had
  1128	assumed, because it seemed from several working examples to be in accord
  1129	with intuition, that once the tightest possible upper and lower bounds
  1130	for a method type parameter have been found, then the union
  1131	(or pseudo-union) of the lower bounds should be chosen as the type to be used for that type parameter.
  1132	% But we were unable to complete the proofs of correctness presented here until we abandoned that assumption.
  1133	% We then considered the hybrid technique of using the intersection of upper bounds only when
  1134	% the union of lower bounds is \Bottom, but we were unable to get that to work either.
  1135	% That is why the dynamic dispatch algorithm presented here always chooses the intersection of the upper bounds.
  1136	% It remains an open question whether there is a provably correct dynamic dispatch technique that
  1137	% chooses the union of the lower bounds.
  1138	We considered this and the hybrid technique of using the intersection of upper bounds only when
  1139	the union of lower bounds is \Bottom, but we were unable to
  1140	complete the proofs of correctness of both the techniques.
  1141	Since the minimum requirement for a type to instantiate a method type parameter
  1142	is that it satisfies all the lower and upper bounds of the type parameter,
  1143	the dynamic dispatch algorithm presented here always chooses
  1144	the intersection of the upper bounds.
  1145	
  1146	In the work presented here, as in previous work, one of the most difficult parts
  1147	is finding the necessary substitution $\sigma$ to satisfy the rule \rncite{E-Sub} for existential
  1148	subtyping during static analysis.  This is more difficult than the corresponding calculation
  1149	during dynamic dispatch because at run time one always matches an ilk (which contains no
  1150	type parameters) to a type, but at compile time one must match a type against a type,
  1151	where each type may contain type parameters.
  1152	Indeed, we do not present a specific static type inference
  1153	algorithm that finds the substitution $\sigma$ in rule \rncite{E-Sub},
  1154	but only refer to previous work in this area.
  1155	However, we conjecture that the \textsf{match} rule presented here can
  1156	serve this role after being extended to handle the case of matching
  1157	two type parameters.

     1	\section{Motivation}\label{sec:motiv}
     2	In this section, we first discuss existing research achievements in
     3	the pursuit of formally defining object-oriented languages with symmetric
     4	multiple dispatch, multiple inheritance, and parametric polymorphism with
     5	variance.  Then, we present how FGFV completes the long-standing endeavor
     6	by defining a core calculus with static overloading rules and a dynamic
     7	dispatch algorithm that are proven type-sound.
     8	
     9	\subsection{Overloading Rules for Multiple Inheritance}\label{sec:motiv:ff}
    10	As we discussed in Section~\ref{sec:intro}, both symmetric multiple
    11	dispatch and multiple inheritance may cause ambiguous method calls
    12	that cannot be resolved at run time.  Let us assume that class $C$ is the only
    13	subtype of both classes $A$ and $B$, and they are all distinct
    14	throughout this section.  Consider
    15	the following overloaded method declarations of $m_1$:
    16	\[\begin{array}[ht]{l@{\hskip2em}l}
    17	\hbox to 12 em{$m_1(x \COLON B, y \COLON C) \COLON B = \cdots$\hfil} & 
    18	\hbox to 12 em{$m_1(x \COLON C, y \COLON B) \COLON B = \cdots$\hfil}
    19	\end{array}\]
    20	which have the same return type $B$ but different domain types
    21	$\tuple{B,C}$ and $\tuple{C,B}$.  For a method invocation $m_1(c, c)$
    22	where the run-time type of $c$ is $C$, it is ambiguous which declaration
    23	to invoke due to symmetric multiple dispatch: both method declarations
    24	are applicable to $(c, c)$ since both $\tuple{B,C}$ and $\tuple{C,B}$ are
    25	supertypes of $\tuple{C,C}$, and neither declaration is more specific
    26	than the other.  Also, consider the following overloaded declarations of
    27	$m_2$:
    28	\[\begin{array}[ht]{l@{\hskip2em}l}
    29	\hbox to 12 em{$m_2(x \COLON A) \COLON \TYP{Boolean} = \cdots$\hfil} &
    30	\hbox to 12 em{$m_2(x \COLON B) \COLON \TYP{Boolean} = \cdots$\hfil}
    31	\end{array}\]
    32	which have domain types $A$ and $B$, respectively.  For a method invocation $m_2(c)$,
    33	it is ambiguous which declaration to invoke due to multiple inheritance:
    34	both declarations are applicable to $c$ and neither declaration is more
    35	specific than the other.
    36	
    37	In order to guarantee that no such ambiguous method calls are possible
    38	at run time, researchers have proposed several calculi with restrictions
    39	on overloaded method declarations.  CF~\cite{ff}, Core Fortress, is a core
    40	calculus of the Fortress programming language~\cite{fortress}, which contains
    41	components, top-level functions, functional methods, and declarations
    42	of exclusive types in addition to multiple inheritance.  However, it
    43	does not specify the language semantics and informally provides rules
    44	for valid overloaded method declarations.  FFMM~\cite{ffcoq},
    45	Featherweight Fortress with Multiple Dispatch and Multiple Inheritance,
    46	simplified CF to focus only on multiple inheritance, and it has a
    47	complete formalization of the language semantics including overloading
    48	rules and its type soundness proof in Coq.  Since the overloading rules
    49	of CF and FFMM are the same, we will refer to these two languages collectively as
    50	\textit{Featherweight Fortress (FF)}.
    51	
    52	The overloading rules of FF require every pair in a set of overloaded
    53	method declarations to satisfy \emph{one} of the following rules:
    54	\begin{description}
    55	\item[\textbf{Exclusion Rule:}] Their domain types are \textit{exclusive}
    56	(their intersection is $\Bottom$, where the $\Bottom$ type is a subtype of every type and
    57	no value belongs to $\Bottom$).
    58	
    59	\item[\textbf{Subtype Rule:}] The domain type of one declaration is
    60	a strict subtype of the domain type of the other, and the return type of
    61	the former is a subtype of the return type of the latter.
    62	
    63	\item[\textbf{Meet Rule:}] The domain types are not exclusive nor in a
    64	subtype relation, and the overloaded set contains a third disambiguating
    65	method declaration which we call the \textit{meet} of the pair.
    66	The meet of two method declarations is more specific than each of the
    67	declarations and less specific than any other method declaration that is
    68	more specific than both declarations.
    69	\end{description}
    70	
    71	Let us revisit the previous examples, with an additional
    72	method declaration each for $m_1$ and $m_2$:
    73	\[
    74	\begin{array}[ht]{@{}l@{$\;$}l@{$\;$}l@{\hskip2.5em}l@{$\;$}l@{$\;$}l@{\hskip2.5em}l@{$\;$}l@{$\;$}l}
    75	d_1^1:\ m_1(x \COLON B, y \COLON C) \COLON B &=& \cdots 
    76	& d_1^2:\ m_1(x \COLON C, y \COLON B) \COLON C &=& \cdots 
    77	& d_1^3:\ m_1(x \COLON C, y \COLON C) \COLON C &=& \cdots \\
    78	d_2^1:\ m_2(x \COLON A) \COLON \TYP{Boolean} &=& \cdots
    79	& d_2^2:\ m_2(x \COLON B) \COLON \TYP{Boolean} &=& \cdots
    80	& d_2^3:\ m_2(x \COLON C) \COLON \TYP{Boolean} &=& \cdots
    81	\end{array}\]
    82	Note that, for both $m_1$ and $m_2$, the third method declaration is the
    83	meet of the first two declarations.
    84	% Each set of overloaded method
    85	% declarations is valid since every pair satisfies one of the overloading
    86	% rules.  For both $m_1$ and $m_2$, the pair of the first two declarations
    87	% satisfies Meet Rule, and the other pairs satisfy Subtype Rule.
    88	Each set of overloaded method
    89	declarations is valid since every pair satisfies one of the overloading
    90	rules (for $i = 1$ and $2$, $d_i^1$ and $d_i^2$ satisfy the Meet Rule; $d_i^1$ and $d_i^3$ satisfy the Return Type Rule, as do $d_i^2$ and $d_i^3$).
    91	
    92	The overloading rules guarantee two important properties: (1) no ambiguous
    93	method calls can occur at run time, and (2) types are preserved even when a
    94	method call is dispatched to a different method declaration at run time
    95	from a method declaration chosen at compile time.  In FF, Exclusion Rule
    96	is for the trivial cases where no ambiguous calls can occur, Meet Rule
    97	%plays an important role for ensuring the existence of a disambiguating method declaration,
    98	ensures the existence of disambiguating method declarations,
    99	and Subtype Rule serves a key role for type
   100	preservation.
   101	
   102	
   103	\subsection{Overloading Rules for Multiple Inheritance and Generics}
   104	\label{sec:motiv:fgf}
   105	Similarly for multiple inheritance, generics may cause ambiguous method
   106	calls that cannot be resolved at run time.  Consider the following
   107	overloaded declarations of $\mbox{\textit{sort}}$:
   108	\[\begin{array}[ht]{l}
   109	\mbox{\textit{sort}}\ob{P \extends A}(x \COLON \kwd{List^I}\ob{P}) \COLON \kwd{SortedList^I}\ob{P}=\cdots\\
   110	\mbox{\textit{sort}}\ob{P \extends B}(x \COLON \kwd{List^I}\ob{P}) \COLON \kwd{SortedList^I}\ob{P}=\cdots\\
   111	\end{array}\]
   112	Their domain types are respectively
   113	``$\kwd{List^I}\ob{P}$ where $P$ is a subtype of $A$''
   114	and ``$\kwd{List^I}\ob{P}$ where $P$ is a subtype of $B$'';
   115	for a method invocation $\mbox{\textit{sort}}(l)$ where the run-time type
   116	of $l$ is $\kwd{List^I}\ob{C}$, both declarations are applicable to $l$ and neither
   117	declaration is more specific than the other.
   118	
   119	In order to support generics as well for symmetric multiple dispatch,
   120	\citet{oopsla11} proposed new overloading rules for given generic
   121	declarations of types and methods.  Even though they did not
   122	present a specific language with generics, we refer to the underlying
   123	language as \textit{FGF}, Featherweight Generic Fortress.
   124	To support generics, the authors
   125	re-defined the terms \emph{applicability} and \emph{specificity} for
   126	generic method declarations and their overloading rules.  A generic
   127	method declaration $d$ is applicable to a type $\alpha$ if there exists
   128	an instance $D$ of $d$ that is applicable to $\alpha$, that is, the
   129	domain type of $D$ is a supertype of $\alpha$.  For example, consider
   130	the following generic method declaration:

1	# Extract: Park, Hong, Steele & Ryu, "Polymorphic Symmetric Multiple Dispatch with Variance" (POPL 2019)
     2	
     3	Working notes on Gyunghee Park (KAIST and Oracle Labs), Jaemin Hong (KAIST),
     4	Guy L. Steele Jr. (Oracle Labs) and Sukyoung Ryu (KAIST), *Polymorphic
     5	Symmetric Multiple Dispatch with Variance*, Proc. ACM Program. Lang. 3, POPL,
     6	Article 11, January 2019, 28 pages, doi:10.1145/3290324. These notes are our
     7	own summary and commentary with brief attributed quotations, not a
     8	reproduction of the paper.
     9	
    10	- **Source.** https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3290324. The PDF,
    11	  https://dl.acm.org/doi/pdf/10.1145/3290324?download=true, was downloaded by
    12	  Pavol on 2026-09-29. It is 28 pages, SHA-256
    13	  `791f978e529b17d533e3342763ed6c54a2f1027eeee5aac9869956b5cdd2b954`.
    14	- **Copies in the repository.** The PDF is `Papers/Variance/3290324-popl19w.pdf`
    15	  (the same SHA-256), beside the team's other papers, and its full text
    16	  (`pdftotext -layout`) is `research/extracts/ParkPOPL2019.txt`, beside these
    17	  notes, so that the paper's
    18	  figures and rules are read at the source.
    19	- **The copy the record read on 2026-09-23** (`explorations/reviews/mie-probes/literature.md`):
    20	  http://web.archive.org/web/20240415191855/https://dl.acm.org/doi/pdf/10.1145/3290324.
    21	- **License**, as printed on the first page: "This work is licensed under a
    22	  Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial 4.0 International License. ©
    23	  2019 Copyright held by the owner/author(s)." That license permits
    24	  copying and redistribution for non-commercial purposes with attribution.
    25	  On that license and because the work needs the paper's figures at the
    26	  source, the curator made it the exception to the rule that keeps copyrighted
    27	  PDFs out of the repository (`explorations/protocol.md`, the hard rules).
    28	
    29	Page numbers are the printed article pages (11:N). The full proofs are in a
    30	companion report, "Polymorphic Symmetric Multiple Dispatch with Variance
    31	(Extended Report)", 2018, which the paper cites without a URL; the paper
    32	itself gives proof sketches. Cross-references to this repository are marked
    33	**[repo]**.
    34	
    35	## 1. What the paper is
    36	
    37	The abstract claims "the first formal specification of a strongly typed
    38	object-oriented language with symmetric multiple dispatch, multiple
    39	inheritance, and parametric polymorphism with variance", with a static and a
    40	dynamic semantics and a type soundness proof "demonstrating that our novel
    41	dynamic dispatch algorithm is consistent with the static semantics"
    42	(p. 11:1). The calculus is **FGFV**, "Featherweight Generic Fortress with
    43	Variance" (p. 11:3). It formalises the overloading rules of the 2011 OOPSLA
    44	paper (Allen et al., in the tree as `Papers/Types/`), which were stated
    45	informally and without a language semantics. It adds declaration-site
    46	variance and a dispatch algorithm, and proves that the static rules and the
    47	run-time choice agree (§6, p. 11:25).
    48	
    49	The language (Fig. 2, p. 11:8; §3.2, pp. 11:8-9):
    50	- **Traits and objects.** Traits are "like Java interfaces that do not have
    51	  any fields", and objects are "like Java final classes that cannot be
    52	  extended".
    53	- **Type parameters.** Trait type parameters carry a variance mark (`+`, `-`,
    54	  `=`) and upper bounds. Object type parameters are always invariant. Method
    55	  type parameters have lower and upper bounds, and the defaults are `Any` and
    56	  `Bottom`.
    57	- **Expressions.** Variables, first-class functions, object creation with
    58	  written type arguments, and method calls `e.m(e)` with no written type
    59	  arguments.
    60	- **Types.** `Bottom` "is intentionally not expressible in the surface
    61	  syntax" (p. 11:9). Union and intersection types exist only as internal
    62	  types (p. 11:9). Tuples are not values.
    63	- **What is left out.** "FGFV omits functional methods … and declarations
    64	  of closed types …, but these could be added back to FGFV in an obvious
    65	  way" (p. 11:3). Related work adds "modularity, nominal exclusion, and
    66	  closed types" to that list (p. 11:25). There are no top-level functions:
    67	  what is overloaded is methods.
    68	
    69	## 2. The rule excluding multiple instantiations
    70	
    71	- **The rule.** Every pair of a class's proper ancestors must satisfy
    72	  [Anc-Diff-Trait] (instances of two different traits: no condition) or
    73	  [Anc-Same-Trait] (Fig. 4, p. 11:11). [D-Trait] and [D-Object] both check it
    74	  (Fig. 3, p. 11:10). [Anc-Same-Trait] requires that "if a class C extends two
    75	  instances of a trait T, T⟦α⟧ and T⟦ρ⟧, then C also extends some T⟦γ⟧
    76	  (which may be T⟦α⟧, T⟦ρ⟧, or a third instance) that extends both"
    77	  (p. 11:11).
    78	- **Per variance (our derivation from the rule's two subtype premises).** An
    79	  invariant parameter forces γ = α = ρ, so two different instances cannot
    80	  both be ancestors: that is the blanket rule. A covariant parameter needs an
    81	  ancestor instance whose argument is below both arguments, and a
    82	  contravariant one needs one whose argument is above both.
    83	- **Why.** "Because the rules guarantee that there always exists a single
    84	  minimal ancestor when a class extends multiple instances of a trait, no
    85	  ambiguous method calls are possible due to multiple instances of a trait"
    86	  (p. 11:11).
    87	- **Credited.** The discussion calls it "the 'Ancestor Meet Rule' …
    88	  introduced into Fortress in 2012 by Guy Steele and David Chase … to design
    89	  an expressive type system with union and intersection types". It gives the
    90	  laws T⟦α ⊓ α′⟧ ≡ T⟦α⟧ ⊓ T⟦α′⟧ for a covariant T and T⟦α ⊔ α′⟧ ≡ T⟦α⟧ ⊓
    91	  T⟦α′⟧ for a contravariant one, and not "the 'obvious other two cases'"
    92	  (p. 11:24). The citation is "Personal communication".
    93	- **Used by the overloading check.** To close part of the gap between
    94	  subtyping of domains and inclusion of applicable sets, the checker reduces
    95	  an existential domain by collecting the constraints that keep it from being
    96	  `Bottom` (*existential reduction*, pp. 11:13-14). The worked case uses
    97	  invariance: with `ArrayList` extending `List` and both invariant, subtypes
    98	  of `ArrayList⟦P⟧` and `List⟦Q⟧` "are exclusive unless they are both
    99	  ArrayList⟦S⟧ for some type S" (pp. 11:13-14). So the rule is what lets
   100	  two generic declarations be proved disjoint or nested.
   101	- **Not argued.** The paper argues that the rule is sufficient, not that it
   102	  is necessary.
   103	
   104	## 3. Variance
   105	
   106	- **Subtyping.** Declaration-site variance on trait type parameters, as in
   107	  the example "T⟦U2, U1, U1⟧ <: T⟦U1, U2, U1⟧" for `trait T⟦+P, -Q, =S⟧` with
   108	  U2 <: U1 (p. 11:9).
   109	- **Positions.** [D-Method] checks that covariant and contravariant class
   110	  type parameters appear only in positions of their own variance. A *type
   111	  context* gives each position a variance: arrow domains and contravariant
   112	  arguments flip it, and "type parameters of objects and invariant type
   113	  parameters of traits are invariant" (pp. 11:11-12).
   114	- **The overloading rules do not change.** "The overloading rules for FGF
   115	  remain the same because covariant or contravariant types affect only the
   116	  well-formedness of method declarations rather than the validity of
   117	  overloading" (p. 11:12).
   118	- **Run time is where variance costs something.** "Supporting variance in a
   119	  type-sound manner requires keeping track of the static types of method
   120	  invocations at run time" (p. 11:7).
   121	  - The example: `sort(x: ListC⟦A⟧)`, `sort(x: ListC⟦B⟧)` and
   122	    `sort⟦P⟧(x: ListC⟦C⟧): SortedListI⟦P⟧`, with `ListC` covariant and
   123	    `SortedListI` invariant, beside a generic
   124	    `merge⟦P⟧(SortedListI⟦P⟧, SortedListI⟦P⟧)`.
   125	  - Two calls statically typed `SortedListI⟦A⟧` feed a merge. If run time
   126	    instantiates the third `sort`'s `P` as anything but `A`, "the merge call
   127	    would fail, despite the fact that the program successfully passed static
   128	    type checking" (p. 11:7).
   129	- **The 2012 alternatives.** The team considered dropping contravariance,
   130	  treating arrow domains as invariant and compensating "by introducing rules
   131	  of coercion". They also considered dropping union types, and perhaps
   132	  intersections, for pseudo-joins and pseudo-meets. The paper instead
   133	  accepts "the potential for exponential blowup" at run time (p. 11:24).
   134	
   135	## 4. How dispatch picks among overloads
   136	
   137	### 4.1 The static rules (§4, pp. 11:12-15)
   138	
   139	- **The reading of a generic declaration.** Following Allen et al. 2011, a
   140	  generic declaration is "a single declaration whose domain type is
   141	  existentially quantified over its type parameters", not "a set of
   142	  infinitely many monomorphic declarations" (p. 11:3). "A monomorphic method
   143	  declaration is a generic method declaration without any type parameter"
   144	  (p. 11:5).
   145	- **Specificity.** The informal rules compare applicable sets, "which is not
   146	  practically checkable", so the formal ones compare domain types by
   147	  subtyping (p. 11:12). This is sound but "not complete" (p. 11:13), and
   148	  existential reduction narrows the gap (§2 above).
   149	- **Three rules for every pair of same-named declarations** (Fig. 5,
   150	  p. 11:13):
   151	  - No Duplicates: the two domains are not each below the other; either
   152	    [No-Dup-Not-Less] or [No-Dup-Not-Gtr] suffices, so the rule refuses
   153	    exactly a pair whose domains are mutual subtypes (p. 11:12).
   154	  - Meet: the domains exclude ([Meet-Excl], their intersection reduces to
   155	    `Bottom`), or one is below the other, or a third declaration's domain is
   156	    equivalent to their intersection ([Meet-Third]).
   157	  - Return Type ([Return-Test]): when d1 is more specific than d2,
   158	    `arrow(d1)` must be a subtype of `∀⟦κ, κ′⟧((α ⊓ α′) → ρ′)`, where the
   159	    κ are both declarations' type parameters, α and α′ their domains and ρ′
   160	    the less specific return type.
   161	- **What [Return-Test] guarantees.** It checks the informal rule "for any
   162	  instance of d2 instantiated with σ2 that is applicable to γ, there exists
   163	  an instance of d1 … that is applicable to γ and has a return type that is
   164	  a subtype of the return type of the instance of d2" (p. 11:15). That is,
   165	  it quantifies over every instance of the less specific declaration.
   166	- **Theorem 4.1** (p. 11:15). "For any method invocation, there always
   167	  exists a unique most specific method declaration in its set of applicable
   168	  method declarations." No Duplicates makes specificity antisymmetric, and
   169	  the Meet Rule gives "a meet for every nonempty subset".
   170	- **Static resolution** ([T-Method], [MSAV], Fig. 7, p. 11:16). The checker
   171	  picks an instance of the most specific declaration applicable to the static
   172	  argument types, and annotates the call with that instance's return type.
   173	  The type-annotated expression `ϵ.m(ϵ): α` is what runs.
   174	
   175	### 4.2 The dynamic choice (§5.2, pp. 11:16-21)
   176	
   177	- **The contract.** "dynamic overloading resolution then must select an
   178	  instance of the most specific method declaration that is applicable to the
   179	  dynamic types of the arguments and whose return type is a subtype of the
   180	  static type of the expression" (p. 11:15).
   181	- **Types at run time.** Types are reified: "all the type parameters are
   182	  instantiated with ground types at run time", and a value's run-time type is
   183	  its *ilk* (p. 11:17). Ground types include unions and intersections
   184	  (Fig. 8, p. 11:17).
   185	- **[R-Method]** (p. 11:17). It sorts the visible declarations most-to-least
   186	  specific ("This order is statically determinable, so the sorting can be
   187	  done at compile time"). It then runs the *dispatch semipredicate* on each
   188	  declaration in turn and takes the first that succeeds. The receiver's ilk is
   189	  matched together with the arguments' ilks, which is what makes the dispatch
   190	  symmetric.
   191	- **The semipredicate** ([Dispatch], pp. 11:17-18) has three steps:
   192	  1. match the argument ilks against the domain to get lower and upper bounds
   193	     for the method type parameters;
   194	  2. match the call's static return type against the declared return type to
   195	     get bounds "to make sure that the dynamic dispatch preserves type";
   196	  3. solve the bounds.
   197	
   198	  "If any of these steps fails, the semipredicate is false: the declaration
   199	  is not applicable" (p. 11:18). Matching a union can yield several candidate
   200	  bound lists, combined as a Cartesian product (pp. 11:18-19).
   201	- **Solving** (Fig. 10, p. 11:19). The rule works from the rightmost type
   202	  parameter to the left and "computes a substitution … by taking the
   203	  intersection of the upper bounds", declared and computed. It then
   204	  propagates the choice into the declared lower bounds of the parameters to
   205	  its left. It "never instantiates method type parameters with Bottom". The
   206	  right-to-left pass works because of the binding restrictions (p. 11:11):
   207	  - a method type parameter's scope "extends to the right of its
   208	    declaration";
   209	  - "no reference to a method type parameter appears in any of the upper
   210	    bounds";
   211	  - the union of the lower bounds must be below the intersection of the upper
   212	    bounds.
   213	- **The worked example** (§5.2.4, pp. 11:20-21).
   214	  - Two covariant `append` declarations, over `SortedList` and over `List`.
   215	  - The call has static type `List⟦C3⟧` and argument ilks `SortedCons⟦C1⟧`
   216	    and `Cons⟦C2⟧`, with C1, C2 <: C3.
   217	  - The `SortedList` declaration fails on the second argument, so the `List`
   218	    one runs, instantiated at `[C3/P, C3/Q]`.
   219	  - So the instance comes from the static return type's upper bound, not from
   220	    the ilks' C1 and C2.
   221	- **Why intersection of upper bounds.** The Fortress team "had assumed …
   222	  that once the tightest possible upper and lower bounds for a method type
   223	  parameter have been found, then the union (or pseudo-union) of the lower
   224	  bounds should be chosen". For that and for a hybrid "we were unable to
   225	  complete the proofs of correctness", so the algorithm "always chooses the
   226	  intersection of the upper bounds" (p. 11:25).
   227	- **Union instances.** A type parameter can be instantiated at a union at
   228	  run time. In the paper's example `O.m(3, true): (Int ⊔ Boolean)`, "P of m
   229	  is inferred as (Int ⊔ Boolean) by the dispatch semipredicate at run time"
   230	  (p. 11:21).
   231	
   232	## 5. The run-time check on the return type
   233	
   234	- **What it is.** Every call carries its static return type into run time
   235	  (§5.1, p. 11:16). Dispatch uses it as an upper bound when it instantiates
   236	  the chosen declaration (p. 11:18).
   237	- **It never moves a call to another declaration.**
   238	  - Lemma 5.8: whatever instance the checker chose, "there exists a
   239	    type-safe most specific method instance at run time" (p. 11:22). Its proof
   240	    is where [Return-Test] is used (pp. 11:22-23).
   241	  - Lemma 5.9: the first-dispatchable scan then yields an instance of the
   242	    most specific declaration applicable to the ilks, with a return type below
   243	    the static one (p. 11:23).
   244	  - In a well-formed program the return-type bounds therefore never rule out
   245	    that declaration. They only choose its instance.
   246	- **What it costs.**
   247	  - "In simple invariant cases, we expect the run-time cost to be relatively
   248	    low but nonzero", since matching `List⟦String⟧` against `List⟦T⟧` only
   249	    binds T (pp. 11:24-25).
   250	  - For the covariant and contravariant cases, "caching or dynamic

250	  - For the covariant and contravariant cases, "caching or dynamic
   251	    recompilation … may help" (p. 11:25).
   252	  - The discussion calls left-to-right scoping "a relatively small sacrifice
   253	    of expressivity for a large gain in dynamic efficiency" (p. 11:24).
   254	
   255	## 6. What it proves and what it leaves open
   256	
   257	**Proved (sketched here, full proofs in the companion report):**
   258	- Theorem 4.1: a unique most specific declaration exists (p. 11:15).
   259	- Soundness and completeness of type matching and of solving (Lemmas 5.1 to
   260	  5.4), and so of the dispatch semipredicate (Theorems 5.5, 5.6;
   261	  pp. 11:21-22). Completeness of matching assumes that a matched type holds
   262	  no `Bottom` and no type parameter inside a union or intersection. The
   263	  paper shows that every use meets this: declared types have neither, and
   264	  unions reach a declaration only through already-ground instances
   265	  (pp. 11:21-22).
   266	- Lemmas 5.7 to 5.9 (pp. 11:22-23).
   267	- Theorem 5.10, soundness of a method call: a well-typed call is reduced by
   268	  [R-Method] and its body's type is below the call's static type (p. 11:23).
   269	- Theorem 5.11, type soundness: if `e` types to `(ϵ, д)` and `ϵ` evaluates to
   270	  a value, the value's type is below `д` (p. 11:24).
   271	- Only the method-invocation case is proved, "the other cases are
   272	  conventional" (p. 11:23). The proofs are not mechanised; the Coq model in
   273	  the lineage is Kim and Ryu 2011, without generics (p. 11:4).
   274	
   275	**Left open or left out:**
   276	- No static inference algorithm: "we do not present a specific static type
   277	  inference algorithm that finds the substitution σ in rule [E-Sub]". The
   278	  paper conjectures that its match rule could serve (p. 11:25).
   279	- Domain subtyping is incomplete against applicable sets (p. 11:13).
   280	- Exponential blowup is possible at run time (p. 11:24).
   281	- The union-of-lower-bounds instance is unproved (p. 11:25).
   282	- Functional methods and top-level functions, closed types (`comprises`),
   283	  nominal exclusion (`excludes`) and modularity are out; the paper says they
   284	  "could be added back … in an obvious way" but shows nothing (pp. 11:3,
   285	  11:25). Self types and a numeric tower are absent: neither is mentioned,
   286	  and `Integer` appears only in a `List⟦Integer⟧` example (p. 11:2).
   287	- Method type parameters may not appear in upper bounds, so F-bounded method
   288	  parameters are outside the calculus (p. 11:11). Trait parameters' bounds are
   289	  checked in an environment that binds the parameters themselves ([D-Trait],
   290	  p. 11:10), so by the rule's form F-bounded trait parameters are admitted.
   291	- Whether the ancestor rule is necessary is not argued.
   292	
   293	## 7. How it differs from the 2012 Welterweight draft and Naden's write-ups
   294	
   295	The paper cites neither text; its only 2012 source is "Steele and Chase 2012.
   296	Personal communication" (p. 11:28). The lineage is by content.
   297	
   298	**Welterweight** (`Papers/Welterweight/`: "Dynamic Dispatch and Type Inference
   299	Semipredicates", Chase, Hilburn, Luchangco, Naden, Ryu, Steele, Tristan,
   300	"PAPER SUBMITTED TO 2012 ACM SPLASH---OOPSLA", `paper.tick:499-509`; Naden
   301	calls it "the failed OOPSLA 2012 submission",
   302	`Papers/Types/journal/justificationOfRTR.tex:538`).
   303	
   304	- *The same:*
   305	  - the Ancestors Meet Rule and its reason, a "unique minimal instance" for
   306	    efficient dispatch (`static.tick:83-89`);
   307	  - ilks;
   308	  - the most-to-least-specific order with a first-success scan of dispatch
   309	    semipredicates (`dispatch.tick:5-20`);
   310	  - right-to-left processing of type parameters under left-to-right scoping
   311	    (`dispatch.tick:67`).
   312	- *The differences:*
   313	  - **Inputs to dispatch.** Welterweight dispatches on the ilks alone: it is
   314	    "possible to select the dynamically most specific applicable function or
   315	    method from an overload set using only the ilks of the argument values; no
   316	    other information about the arguments is needed" (`evaluation.tick:30-33`).
   317	    POPL adds the call's static return type.
   318	  - **The instance.** Welterweight aims at "the most specific instantiation"
   319	    by propagating lower limits (`dispatch.tick:67`). It leaves the Return
   320	    Type Rule to "one final adjustment step … after the entrypoint [has] been
   321	    chosen", with no static type to adjust to (`dispatch.tick:212`). POPL
   322	    takes the intersection of the upper bounds, the static return type among
   323	    them.
   324	  - **Proof.** Welterweight states soundness as propositions that "should
   325	    also hold" if "our type system is sound" (`evaluation.tick:71-99`). POPL
   326	    proves them.
   327	  - **Language.** Welterweight's is larger: top-level functions, a typecase
   328	    (`R-Match-Succeeds`), `comprises` and `excludes` clauses, and coverage of
   329	    abstract declarations. POPL drops all of these. POPL does handle
   330	    contravariance and intersections in matching, where Welterweight's main
   331	    algorithm is "Simplified version: no contravariance or ∩", with
   332	    contravariance a variation (`dispatch.tick:62`, `:365`).
   333	  - **Self types.** Welterweight's self-typed-generics dispatch step is
   334	    commented out (`dispatch.tick:195-210`); POPL has no self types at all.
   335	
   336	**Naden, "The Return Type Rule and Generics"** (2012-08-31,
   337	`Papers/Types/journal/justificationOfRTR.tex`).
   338	- *Rejected:* letting the static context limit which definitions are
   339	  applicable, so that overloads failing the Return Type Rule could pass.
   340	  "By adding contextual information to the concept of the overload set, we
   341	  muddy its semantics" (`:241-305`, quoted at `:289-290`).
   342	- *Kept:* the Return Type Rule, plus multiple instantiation exclusion: "any
   343	  type which is a subtype of two distinct instantiations of a single generic
   344	  type is equivalent to Bottom" (`:342-347`), with a proof (`:433`).
   345	- *Why:* a canonical instance for run-time choice (`headOrID`, "Context
   346	  does not give us any clue", `:480-495`). So "Fortress implements blanket
   347	  multiple instantiation exclusion" (`:496`).
   348	- *For covariant parameters:* a minimal instance suffices, "the ancestor
   349	  meet rule that appears in the failed OOPSLA 2012 submission" (`:512-538`).
   350	  He adds a second, cross-instantiation restriction between a covariant
   351	  subtrait and its supertrait (`:540-566`). He finds that the numeric tower's
   352	  self-type idiom breaks it, and that "more work needs to be done"
   353	  (`:568-633`). His suggested rewrite puts the self type in a bound,
   354	  `add⟦X <: Ring⟦X⟧⟧(X, X): X` (`:620-624`).
   355	
   356	**Naden, "Enforcing Fortress' Return Type Rule at Runtime"** (2012-08-31,
   357	`Papers/RuntimeInstantiation/RTRinstantionTheory.tex`, with the notes of
   358	May to July 2012 beside it).
   359	- *Proposed:* adding bounds from the call's static return type to run-time
   360	  instantiation "without changing which function definition will be chosen"
   361	  (`:73-80`).
   362	- *Proved:* a theorem that under the Return Type Rule the return-type bounds
   363	  are satisfiable exactly when applicability is, so they can join the
   364	  single pass (`:279-298`).
   365	- *Not done:* the bound-generation algorithm and the open coding (`:84-89`).
   366	
   367	**POPL 2019 against these.**
   368	- It carries out the second write-up in a full calculus, with proofs: the
   369	  return-type bounds in the semipredicate, and Lemmas 5.8 and 5.9.
   370	- It stays within the first write-up's position: overload sets are validated
   371	  statically and without context, the Return Type Rule is kept, and the
   372	  exclusion rule is kept with the covariant relaxation, extended to
   373	  contravariance.
   374	- It does not do what that write-up rejected: the static type chooses the
   375	  instance, never the declaration (§5 above). One part of Naden's objection
   376	  still applies to the instance: which instance runs depends on static
   377	  information (the `append` example).
   378	- It has no counterpart to the cross-instantiation restriction. Whether
   379	  [Return-Test] refuses Naden's `coTail` pair instead has not been worked
   380	  out here.
   381	- It says nothing on the tower problem.
   382	- It excludes the F-bounded method parameters of Naden's suggested rewrite
   383	  (§6).
   384	
   385	## 8. Bearing on the decisions on record
   386	
   387	- **Instantiation exclusion and route A (POSITIONS 2026-09-24).**
   388	  - [Anc-Same-Trait] is the rule route A keeps: blanket for invariant
   389	    parameters, as rung S states it in Luchangco's two-part form
   390	    (`Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick:353-360`).
   391	  - For covariant parameters the two are consistent by our reading: the
   392	    Types chapter lets two instances share a value unless their covariant
   393	    arguments exclude, and the paper asks a class with both to have an
   394	    instance below both. The Types chapter has only `covariant`; the paper
   395	    also has contravariance.
   396	  - The record summarises the route as "culminating in the POPL 2019 paper,
   397	    which keeps the rule and specialisation by a run-time return-type check,
   398	    with no self types and no tower". The full text bears that out (§§2, 5,
   399	    6).
   400	  - The paper uses the rule inside the overloading check (existential
   401	    reduction, pp. 11:13-14). That is the same work instantiation exclusion
   402	    does in the checker's domain reduction
   403	    (`reviews/overloading-judgement.md` § 3.5).
   404	  - **[repo]** The rule was in the checker from 2010 (FACTS, the exclusion
   405	    fork, dated). The paper's 2012 date is for the ancestor form.
   406	- **Answer 9's overloading rules (POSITIONS 2026-09-26).**
   407	  - The paper is answer 9's model, formalised and proved: existential
   408	    domains, the plain declaration as the degenerate case, the three rules,
   409	    and specificity by domain subtyping (§4.1).
   410	  - Calls write no static arguments (Fig. 2). So answer 9's positional rule,
   411	    which exists for calls that do, has no counterpart. That fits answer 9's
   412	    note on the 2011 paper.
   413	  - The paper overloads methods only. Fortress's top-level functions and
   414	    operators are, by our reading, the receiver-free case.
   415	- **The return-type rule over every instance (answer 9, defect 2).**
   416	  [Return-Test] is exactly the construction answer 9 prescribes for the
   417	  checker rung, the "special arrow" `∀[Δ1, Δ2] (S1 ∩ S2) → T2` with the less
   418	  specific declaration's parameters kept quantified
   419	  (`reviews/overloading-judgement.md` § 3.5). The paper states that it
   420	  covers every instance of the less specific declaration (p. 11:15), and
   421	  its universal reduction is the paper's form of "except where the domain
   422	  reduction forces an equality" (pp. 11:14-15). The rung can cite Fig. 5 and
   423	  Fig. 6 as its specification.
   424	- **Run-time instantiation of a dispatched generic (item 30, POSITIONS
   425	  2026-09-29).** The decision: the generic declaration runs, at the instance
   426	  the value fixes, and at the least instance within the bounds where it fixes
   427	  none; Naden's return-type restriction is future work
   428	  (`reviews/plain-beside-generic-judgement.md:74`, `:159`).
   429	  - *Which declaration:* the paper agrees. The most specific declaration
   430	    applicable to the ilks runs (Lemma 5.9).
   431	  - *Naden's restriction:* the paper is its published, proved form (§§5, 7).
   432	  - *The instance where the value does not fix it:* the paper diverges. It
   433	    takes the intersection of the upper bounds, declared and from the static
   434	    return type (p. 11:19), and reports that the least instance, the union
   435	    of the lower bounds, could not be proved correct (p. 11:25). Item 30's
   436	    default is Welterweight's "most specific instantiation"
   437	    (`dispatch.tick:67`), which is that unproved choice.
   438	  - *Where the value fixes it* (an invariant position), the two agree.
   439	  - *An example* (ours, by reading, not run): `wrap[\X extends Number\](x:
   440	    X): Box[\X\]` beside `wrap(a: Any): Any` is a valid pair (the generic is
   441	    more specific, and its return type is below `Any`). Called through a
   442	    variable of type `Any` holding a `ZZ32`, item 30's default runs it at
   443	    `ZZ32` and returns a `Box[\ZZ32\]`. The paper's rule runs it at `Number`,
   444	    the declared bound, since the static return type `Any` adds nothing, and
   445	    returns a `Box[\Number\]`.
   446	  - *Unions:* the paper also instantiates at run-time unions (p. 11:21),
   447	    which the compiled path does not have (item 30's judgement, line 74).
   448	  - Both points should reach the coordinator before batch 7b's rung S writes
   449	    item 30's sentence.
   450	- **The `covariant` keyword (row 404, POSITIONS 2026-09-26).**
   451	  - FGFV is the formal account of the 2012 `covariant` and `contravariant`
   452	    modifiers: position checks, the ancestor rule relaxed by variance, and
   453	    overloading rules unchanged.
   454	  - It also says what carrying variance to run time takes beyond
   455	    variance-aware subtyping of reified types: the static return type at
   456	    every call (p. 11:7).
   457	  - It is the design reference for worklist item 12 when that is taken up.
   458	    It changes nothing in row 404's standing as future work off the path to
   459	    microGPT.
   460	  - Its variance is on type parameters only. Sign flags as covariant
   461	    parameters (probe `Q3Phantom`) would be an extension.
   462	- **`comprises` read on values (item 26, POSITIONS 2026-09-29).**
   463	  - The paper has no closed types, so it says nothing on reading a
   464	    `comprises` clause, and its "obvious" addition is not shown.
   465	  - Its Meet Rule asks for a declaration whose domain is equivalent to the
   466	    intersection ([Meet-Third]), and Theorem 4.1 gives a unique most specific
   467	    declaration for static types and ilks alike. So it keeps static
   468	    uniqueness, the property item 26 gives up for closed traits in favour of
   469	    run-time uniqueness.
   470	  - What it shares with item 26's rung W is the run-time shape: a statically
   471	    sorted most-to-least-specific list scanned for the first fit (p. 11:17;
   472	    `explorations/coordinator/PLAN.md`, batch 7b's line on item 26).
   473	  - Its proofs are over a whole program, so the closure caveat of row 487 has
   474	    no counterpart.
   475	- **F-bounded functions in the library (no decision yet; for batch 8 and the
   476	  switch-over).** Generic functions such as
   477	  `opr BIG MIN[\T extends StandardMin[\T\]\](g: Generator[\T\]): T`
   478	  (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:1929`) are outside FGFV on two counts: they
   479	  are top-level operators, and their type parameter appears in its own upper
   480	  bound (restriction (2), p. 11:11).

# Gyunghee Park, "Polymorphic Symmetric Multiple Dispatch with Variance" (POPL 2019)

## The talk

### Slide 1 of 21: Polymorphic Symmetric Multiple Dispatch with Variance

> Polymorphic Symmetric Multiple Dispatch with Variance
>
> Gyunghee Park, Jaemin Hong, Guy L. Steele Jr., Sukyoung Ryu (the speaker's name in bold); POPL'19

**Session chair (0:05):** […] Dispatch with Variance, and Gyunghee Park is going to give the talk.

**Gyunghee Park (0:10):** Yeah. Thank you for the introduction. Yeah, this talk is about Polymorphic Symmetric Multiple Dispatch with Variance. I'm Gyunghee Park, and it's a joint work with Jaemin Hong, Guy Steele, and Sukyoung Ryu.

### Slide 2 of 21: Method Overloading

> - Allows multiple method declarations with the same name
> - `add(a: Int, b: Int): Int = ⋯`
> - `add(a: Int, b: Int, c: Int): Int = ⋯`
> - `add(a: List, b: List): List = ⋯`
> - `add(a: SortedList, b: SortedList): SortedList = ⋯`
> - Diagram: List above SortedList.
> - Builds: `a: List = SortedList(2, 7)`, `b: SortedList = SortedList(1, 3, 5)`, `add(a, b)`. Arrows from the call to all four declarations. With the static types List and SortedList boxed, "Static overloading resolution" keeps one arrow, to `add(a: List, b: List)`. With the values boxed, "Dynamic overloading resolution / Dynamic dispatch" keeps one arrow, to `add(a: SortedList, b: SortedList)`.

(0:26) As you all may know, method overloading allows multiple method declarations with the same name. So the methods that logically perform very similar tasks can be defined with the same name, but with different names of parameters or different types of parameters.

Let's assume SortedList extends List, and we have these four add method declarations. And let's say we have two variables, a and b, with static types of List and SortedList and dynamic types of both SortedList. For an add method call with a and b as arguments, the language needs to decide which method declaration to invoke among the overloaded methods.

At compile time, static overloading resolution chooses a method to invoke based on the static types of the arguments. And at run time, dynamic overloading resolution or dynamic dispatch chooses a method to invoke based on the run-time types of the arguments.

### Slide 3 of 21: Dynamic Dispatch

> - Selects a method to call among overloaded methods at run time
> - `add(a: List, b: List): List = ⋯`
> - `add(a: List, b: SortedList): List = ⋯`
> - `add(a: SortedList, b: List): List = ⋯`
> - `a: List = SortedList(2, 7)`, `b: SortedList = SortedList(1, 3, 5)`, `add(a, b)`; List above SortedList.
> - Builds, each replacing the bullet:
>   - "Single dispatch: based on a single argument (receiver)". The static types point to `add(a: List, b: SortedList)`. The value of a, `SortedList(2, 7)`, points to the second and third declarations, then to `add(a: List, b: SortedList)` alone.
>   - "Asymmetric multiple dispatch: based on more than one arguments in a specific order (left to right)". Both values point to all three declarations, then to `add(a: SortedList, b: List)` alone.
>   - "Symmetric multiple dispatch: based on more than one arguments considering them equally". Both values point to all three declarations. A fourth is added, `add(a: SortedList, b: SortedList): SortedList = ⋯`, and the call points to it alone. In orange: "Can support binary methods intuitively and uniformly".

(1:30) Let's now consider a slightly different set of overloaded method to see different kinds of dynamic dispatch. So the parameter types are now List List, List SortedList, and SortedList List.

First one, single dynamic dispatch chooses a method to invoke based on the run-time type of a single argument, which usually is the receiver. So in a language with single dispatch, static overloading resolution is used to disambiguate among the overloaded methods. And then at run time, by looking at the run-time type of the receiver, variable a in this case, it first determines which class it belongs to. And then among the overloaded and possibly overridden methods, it chooses an appropriate one that was determined at compile time.

Asymmetric multiple dispatch chooses a method to invoke based on the run-time types of more than one arguments in a specific order, which usually is left to right order. So among the method declarations that are applicable to the run-time types of the arguments, it chooses the most specific one by considering the parameter types in left to right order.

The last one, symmetric multiple dispatch, chooses a method to invoke based on the run-time types of more than one argument, but here by considering all of them equally. So, yeah, but in this case, since neither of the second and the third declaration is more specific than the other, we need another disambiguating method declaration. And since the last one is the most specific method declaration applicable to the run-time argument types, this method call is dispatched to this last declaration. Okay. Oh, sorry.

As you've seen in these examples, compared to other kinds of dynamic dispatch, symmetric multiple dispatch makes an intuitive and uniform choice among the overloaded methods. However, there is no free lunch, and there are a few things to take into account when the language supports symmetric multiple dispatch.

### Slide 4 of 21: Issues in Symmetric Multiple Dispatch

> - `m1(x: B, y: C): B = ⋯`
> - `m1(x: C, y: B): C = ⋯`
> - Diagram: B above C.
> - `m1(c1, c2)`. c1: static type C, run-time type C. c2: static type B, run-time type C.

# Pavol's type decisions, read as one chain: the judgement

## 0. Words

Each term of type theory is defined here once, with a Fortress example where one helps; the verdicts use them without further definition.

- **Type, subtype.** A type is a set of values; `A` is a subtype of `B` when every `A` is a `B`. Under route A, `ZZ32` is not a subtype of `ZZ64` (F-131).
- **Trait, object, extends.** A trait is an interface that may carry method bodies; an object is a leaf type. `trait Vector[\T, nat s0\] extends { AnyVector, Array1[\T,0,s0\], AdditiveGroup[\Vector[\T,s0\]\] }` says every vector is an array and an additive group (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:1616-1618`).

content.content:
## 1. The verdicts, in order of consequence

### V1. The chain bends in one place that matters: P-146's signature half forces P-157, and P-157 overrules the team's library on a conflict that is the checker's, not the library's.

P-157 gives up `Vector` and `Matrix` as additive groups because "the scalar block that microGPT uses (P-88) and the team's additive-group vectors cannot both pass the overload check while it reads a self-typed trait's `self` in a signature as the plain trait type (P-146)" (POSITIONS P-157). Four facts, each checked at its source, turn this from a library decision into a checker gap:

1. The pair is valid under the designers' own rules. A vector is an `Array[\T,ZZ32\]` (`Array1` extends `StandardMutableArrayType`, which extends `Array[\E,I\]`: `FortressLibrary.fsi:1591-1593`, `:1522-1523`, the same at `a874948ac:1435-1437`, `:1371-1372`) and an `AdditiveGroup[\Vector[\T,s0\]\]`. For a value to lie in both the scalar block's domain `(Array[\T,I\], T)` and `AdditiveGroup`'s `(AdditiveGroup[\V\], V)`, the second argument must be a `T` (a `Number`) and a `V`; its bounds make it an `AdditiveGroup[\T\]` and an `AdditiveGroup[\V\]`, so by instantiation exclusion `V = T`; the first argument is then an `Array` and an `AdditiveGroup[\T\]`, and by P-146's extender rule every `AdditiveGroup[\T\]` value is a `T`, a `Number`, which arrays exclude (`:1594`). The domains exclude. The two steps the checker's exclusion test lacks are exactly these: reading a parameter's bounds, and reading the extender rule's fact. The probe's `VecPairsC` says exactly this: the pair is "valid only by the self-type conformance" and "the overload check reads the plain trait type (P-146)" (`perf-probes/symbolic-operators-2/REPORT.md:166`); its left-hand mirror needs the exclusion test to read bounds, row 786's open gap (`:168`).
2. The team had both. At `a874948ac` the library declares `Vector ... extends { ..., AdditiveGroup[\Vector[\T,s0\]\] }` (`:1459-1460`) beside `opr +(x: Array[\ZZ32,ZZ32\], y: ZZ32)` (`:2537`). The evidence map's "the team never had both" (`evidence.md:217`, `:587`) is true only of the generic block; the team's concrete pair has the shape of `VecPairsC`, which the probe found refused, so by that reading, not measured on the team's library, the checker would refuse the team's own library. The conflict is between the team's library and the checker's exclusion reasoning, not between the revival's extension and the team's design.
3. The team's compiled world would have accepted it. Under the team's idiom `comprises T`, the checker types `self` in the signature as `(T[\U\] & {U})` (`XXX10k.test:13-29`, cited in `reviews/self-typed-bodies-judgement.md:20`), and with `self: AdditiveGroup[\V\] & V` the domains exclude at once. P-146 chose the intersection in bodies only and the plain trait type in signatures (POSITIONS P-146; `Specification/appendices/changes.tex:3949-3953`).
4. The two reasons for the signature half do not carry it. The first, that POPL 2019's proofs "assume that no declared type holds a type parameter inside an intersection", is the paper's Lemma 5.2 on type matching at run-time dispatch (`research/extracts/ParkPOPL2019.txt:1098-1107`); it is a silence about FGFV's syntax (declared types there have no intersections at all), and it bears on the dynamic dispatcher's completeness in phase 5, not on the static exclusion test of the Meet Rule, which is where the vectors' pair fails. The second, the 18 Return Type errors on `CMP` (`changes.tex:3997-4004`), was traced by the judgement's own measurement to a checker mechanic: `providedAndOverridden` pairs an overriding `CMP` with the one it overrides as equals and checks the Return Type Rule in both directions (`self-typed-bodies-judgement.md:197-202`; `STypesUtil.scala:1663-1671`, `OverloadingChecker.scala:672-674`). An override whose return type narrows is not a Return Type error; the errors are an artifact of the override check, not of the intersection.

So P-146's body half and extender rule finish a design the team pointed at (Naden's "only in bounds", `Papers/Types/journal/justificationOfRTR.tex:626-630`; the checker's own 2009 self type), while its signature half departs from the team's compiled idiom on a silence and an artifact, and that departure is the sole reason P-157 overrules the team's library and parks P-28's algebra further off. His yes to P-157 rested on the premise that his own extension was being reverted (`POSITIONS-history.md`, P-157's block; `evidence.md:215`). **P-157 should wait; the way back is a checker change, not a library change** (section 2, item 2; section 4, change 1).

### V2. P-156's tuple rule is a departure from the designers' type text, not "the team's magic read as subtyping"; the `Index` bound itself finishes the team's wish.

The team wrote: "We want to say that the type variable I extends a type, say, Index which either excludes Range[I] or is a supertype of Range[I]. However, we cannot say that because ... we write a[1, 2, 3] where the arguments are passed as a tuple ... we need a magic to convert that tuple argument expression to something of type Index" (`Specification-1.0-frozen/appendices/future.tex:198-207`). The bound is their wish; the tuple rule, "a tuple type whose elements are all `Index` types is itself an `Index`" (P-156), makes a tuple type a subtype of a trait type, which the Working Draft forbids three times (`types-vals-vars.tex:214-215`, `:265`, `:272-273`) and the 2012 Types chapter, their latest word on types, forbids twice (`types.tick:341`, `:424`); the revised specification still carries two of those sentences (`Specification/basic/types-vals-vars.tex:232`, `:323-324`), and the checker encodes it (`TypeAnalyzer.scala:560`, which the probe's patch left contradicting its own subtyping rule: "its checker says a tuple is an Index and also excludes it", the coordinator at 06:49 UTC, `evidence.md:208`). The team's word "convert" points at a conversion, and the probe found a conversion would change every index value (`REPORT.md:201`). So this is a point the designers left open (`evidence.md`, Part 4, item 11), on which every way departs somewhere: S5 is a `where` form the team listed only as an open question (`future.tex:209-212`) and is not among the Working Draft's seven constraint forms (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/trait-parameters.tex:319-331`); W3 takes slicing from the generic views; S2 breaks P-45's every-instance rule; S4 changes microGPT's string slicing (`run-c4/src/FlatData.fss:34`, `:54`). The tuple rule is the least costly, and it is a language change that contradicts two designers' texts. **It stands as the choice, with its recording and its checker side changed before it lands** (section 2, item 1).

### V3. Walk's half of conditional extension (row 774) should wait: by the logic of the revival's own rules for walk, and because row 364 makes the fix wrong under walk today.

P-12 and P-59 leave walk unchanged, before it runs the checker after the switch-over, where the matter is one of static types that walk does not have (POSITIONS P-12, P-59, each stated for coercion); the same logic covers this one. Conditional extension is such a matter: the checker reads the condition at a declaration's static arguments (F-255). Walk instantiates a list at its elements' run-time class, `<|1, 2|>` at `List[\Int\]` (row 364), and `Int` is a `StandardTotalOrder[\ZZ32\]`, not `[\Int\]`, so the shadow of the fix takes the order from every unwritten list of numerals or strings: 10 interpreter tests red, 4 of them the team's, and the team's specification example (`perf-probes/walk-conditional-extension/REPORT.md:11-16`, `:66-82`). That is not P-154's intended loss; it is row 364's. Mechanism B, the library's `=/=` and `assert` reaching a list's `=` only through `LexicographicOrder`, is a defect of today's tree (`:174-181`), cleared by the library's own way for `Map`, `IntMap` and `PrefixMap`, `List extends Equality[\List[\E\]\]` (`:99-113`). **The walk rung waits; the `Equality` line lands now; the `=/=` defect is filed** (section 2, item 3).

### V4. P-154 stands on its merits, with its reason corrected: the team's own `LexicographicOrder` body needs ordered elements, the team's `List` extends it at every element type, and conditional extension is the mechanism the team named.

The team's `LexicographicOrder[\T extends LexicographicOrder[\T,E\], E\]` leaves `E` unbounded and its body computes `a CMP b` on `E` values as a `TotalComparison` (`a874948ac:Library/FortressLibrary.fss:1735-1741`), which only an ordered `E` provides; the team's `List[\E\]` extends it for every `E` (`a874948ac:Library/List.fsi:67`). So the team's text is inconsistent with itself, which walk hid by having no static types. Bounding `E` (`372b9bf6a`) and extending `List` conditionally reconciles the two texts by the mechanism the team wished it had explored, "conditional inheritance via where clauses" (`research/extracts/fortress-websites-wayback.md:124-126`). P-154's stated reason, "the team's later code bounds the element of both of its lexicographic traits by a total order" (`Library/incomplete/advanced/Fortress.PartialTotalOrders.fss:117-140`), is backwards in time: those traits are of 2007-2008 and incomplete (`evidence.md:243`), while the live `List` is of 2012. The decision is right; its recorded reason is wrong, and should be the reconciliation above. A cost P-154 accepted knowingly: QuickCheck, team code, keys a map by lists of `Any` (`Library/QuickCheck.fss:1069`, `:1080-1082`), which relied on walk's lack of types.

### V5. The roots and route A stand; the earlier review's verdict on them is confirmed, and nothing since moves it.

- P-26 **Where the type group's later positions conflict with the specification's early text, the later positions win.** The early text was a wish. The type group, the part of the team that built the type checker and the compiler, then worked to make the language run, with performance as the goal and specialization a must, and learned what is feasible. Specialization, in the type group's design, is a special version of a generic function for one instantiation, such as `tail(x: List[ZZ])` beside `tail[X](x: List[X])`, which dispatch chooses at run time. Where the two conflict, the specification is revised to follow their later word (P-95 records each change with its reason). Their later word includes the exclusion rule, specialization kept, the number types of the compiler's prelude made siblings in 2009 and 2010 (P-43: the library's numbers are flat in the same way), Karl Naden's 2012 write-up "The Return Type Rule and Generics" (`Papers/Types/journal/justificationOfRTR.tex`) and the type group's POPL 2019 paper with its technical report, the team's last word and work, kept in `Papers/` with their other papers (F-166; F-300). == explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### The one library and the compiled checker

POSITIONS.md:42
- P-45 **Overloaded declarations may differ in their static parameters.** The specification drops its sentence that forbids this, and keeps it as superseded text. It states instead the overloading model of the type group's 2011 paper (`Papers/Types/`), which the compiled checker already used. The checker keeps the paper's three rules: No Duplicates, Meet and Return Type. It checks the Return Type Rule over every instance of a generic declaration that the argument types allow, not over one guessed instance. One rule of the old sentence survives: if one generic declaration is more specific than another, their static parameters must line up position by position, as Java's rule for overriding a generic method requires. The compiled checker tests it only where the two declarations have as many static parameters of their own (F-75). Walk chooses among overloads by the parameter types that each declaration declares, not by the order in which they are written. At load, walk judges each pair of two generic declarations by the checker's rules on their declared parameter types. It does not refuse a pair only because none of their parameter types exclude, as when one declaration is more specific than the other. Walk and the checker must accept the same pairs. The library repairs, by declarations of its own, the overload sets that the checker refused, and no line of microGPT's two programs changes. Where walk or the checker still judges a pair against these rules: walk compares two functional methods of a generic trait or object on the instance that a call makes (F-26); both paths refuse the paper's own valid example (row 539); walk refuses two generic functional methods of a trait without static parameters whose declared domains lie one inside the other, and fails at a call on such a pair in a generic trait (rows 779 and 780); and walk and the checker disagree on four kinds of pair (rows 759 and 786 to 788).

POSITIONS.md:45
- P-48 **A type parameter that a call's arguments do not fix takes its bound, never `Bottom`.** The arguments leave a parameter unfixed when it occurs only in the result type; when two arguments meet at it with no narrowest type into which both convert (a `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64` have one, `ZZ64`, by P-74); or when dispatch, at run time, picks a generic declaration and must choose the instance to run. Its instance is then the intersection of its upper bounds (`Any` if it has none). At checking, that is narrowed by what the call's expected type (P-49 defines it) requires of the declared return type; at run time, by the static type that the checker gave the call. It is never `Bottom`, never the union of the arguments' types, and never the value's type alone. The rule sets the instance, not which declaration runs (P-46). Why: the rule is the team's later word, from the POPL 2019 paper on multiple dispatch, and the curator trusts the team's later work above his own understanding. The rule changes nothing in microGPT, whose types are concrete. The library keeps the team's declarations of `fail`, `builtinPrimitive` and `List`'s empty comprehension, whose type parameters have no written bound, without the `extends Object` that a batch had added. Under walk, which has no static types, dispatch takes the value's type. Row 538: a compiled dispatcher that carries the static type that the checker gave the call, so that a generic declaration reached only at run time gets this instance. Rows 587, 591 and 612: three cases in which walk still gives `Bottom`.

POSITIONS.md:59
- P-146 **In a self-typed trait, the compiled checker types `self` in the method bodies as also being the implementing type.** A self-typed trait is a trait `C[\X\]` whose parameter `X` extends `C[\X\]`, such as `Integral[\I extends Integral[\I\]\]`. In its method bodies, `self` has the type `C[\X\] & X`. The method signatures keep the plain trait type, because the proofs of the POPL 2019 paper on multiple dispatch (Park, Hong, Steele and Ryu) assume that no declared type holds a type parameter inside an intersection. Only the overloading check's exclusion test reads `self` in a signature as `C[\X\] & X` (P-157). The checker refuses a type that extends such a trait at another type, since an extender must be a subtype of the static argument that it gives: `object Bad extends Integral[\ZZ32\]` is refused, because `Bad` is not a `ZZ32`. Scala has the same rule for self types. The library's text gains no self type and no `comprises` clause, and walk is unchanged. The rule accepts every self-typed method body of the library except `Integral`'s `numerator`, which each integer type declares instead. Why: the checker reads the library as the team wrote it, as P-44 does for the closure of `AnyIntegral`, by one rule that peer languages share. F-225 states the rule as built.

POSITIONS.md:67
- P-156 **A collection's index type extends `Index`, a trait that the ranges exclude, and a tuple of indices is an `Index`.** Every index parameter of the library's generic indexed types is bounded `I extends Index`; `ZZ32` extends `Index`, and `Range` excludes it. So a subscript that takes one index and a subscript that takes a range never apply to the same value, and the pair is a valid overloading at every instance. A tuple type whose elements are all `Index` types is itself an `Index`, on both paths and in the specification: a typing rule that changes no value, so `m[i, j]` passes its tuple `(i, j)` as before. Why: it is the team's own fix for this pair (`Specification/appendices/future.tex:186-207`), its "magic" read as subtyping. A `where` constraint `I excludes Range[\I\]` was weighed and not taken: the team left such a constraint as an open question, and the code generator refuses a `where` clause in a declaration's header. `Index` stands beside `Any` and `Object`, outside `Object`: it is declared `trait Index extends Any`, which the desugaring and walk keep as written and the traits chapter names as an exception to the rule that every trait extends `Object`, so a tuple of indices is an `Index` and never an `Object`, and P-42's tuples stay out of `Object`, as the specification's `trait Tuple extends Any excludes { Object }` keeps them. `BoundedRange`, which cannot take the bound, since the open range `(:)` stays a range over `Any` (P-56), keeps its narrowed `atMost(n: I): FullRange[\I\]` under the method condition `where { I extends Index }`, the library's form for a member that applies at some instances only; after the switch-over the code generator's refusal of a method with a `where` clause stops it too, as it stops `SumReduction`'s two `distribute`s (row 701). Row 783: the subscript pair.

POSITIONS.md:68
- P-157 **`Vector` and `Matrix` stay additive groups, and the overloading check's exclusion test reads the self type and the static parameters' bounds, so the arrays' scalar `+` and `-` stand beside the vectors' own.** The team's `Vector` and `Matrix` extend `AdditiveGroup`, and the library's generic block of `+`, `-`, `MIN` and `MAX` between an array and a scalar (P-88) stays beside them. With symbolic operators checked (P-155), the checker refused 8 such pairs, though no call fits both: a vector's own `+` takes two vectors, the block's `+` an array and a number, and arrays exclude numbers. So the exclusion test reads a self-typed trait's `self` as `C[\X\] & X`, the fact that P-146's extender rule guarantees, and its existential reduction reads the static parameters' bounds (P-152); specificity and the Return Type Rule keep the plain signatures. Why: it keeps both the team's library as written and the revival's block, and it was his first stance; taking vectors out of `AdditiveGroup` would have bent the team's design for a gap of the checker. Reading bounds is the POPL 2019 paper's own reduction. Probe A1 measured it (`perf-probes/self-type-exclusion/REPORT.md`): the 8 gone, nothing else moved.
