POSITIONS.md:40
- P-43 **The exclusion rule stays, and the number tower is flat (route A).** The compiled checker keeps the multiple instantiation exclusion rule. So the library's numbers are flat, as the team (Chase, Ryu, Maessen and Allen) flattened the compiler prelude in 2009 and 2010. The fixed widths, `ZZ`, `QQ` and `RR64` are siblings under `Number`, each with its own algebra, and `Number` has no catch-all operators. Why: the flattened prelude is the team's last record of the Fortress way, and its route leads to the POPL 2019 paper, which keeps the rule. He cares that specialised code runs fast, not how a specialisation is chosen. F-46 prices a return to route C.

POSITIONS.md:64
- P-152 **Walk and the compiled checker read the exclusion of two generic declarations over their whole parameter types, by existential reduction.** With static parameters, the parameter types of two declarations can exclude each other as a whole, even where no single parameter excludes its counterpart. In `o[\T\](x: P[\T\], b: Box[\T\])` beside `o[\T\](x: Q[\T\], b: Box[\T\])`, where `P[\T\]` excludes `Q[\T\]` only at the same `T`, neither parameter excludes alone. But no value is a `Box` of two types, so `b` fixes the same `T` for both declarations, and no argument fits both. A generic trait in `Box`'s place fixes `T` in the same way. Both paths read such a pair as excluding, and judge it on that reading by the overloading rules (P-45: the 2011 paper's No Duplicates, Meet and Return Type rules). Why: the type group's 2011 paper decides exclusion between parameter types with static parameters by existential reduction (`Papers/Types/exc-reduction.tick`), as the revised specification states (`Specification/advanced/overloading.tex`, "Declarations with Static Parameters"). Walk refuses such a pair at load where one declaration has a `where` clause, which the checker accepts (row 787); and walk reads an object type over a static parameter, such as `Box[\T\]`, as excluding a type that it equals at some instance, such as `Box[\ZZ32\]`, so that it loads a pair that the checker refuses (row 788).

POSITIONS.md:57
- P-60 **The specification reads a `comprises` clause at the level of values.** `trait S comprises { U, V }` says that every value of `S` is a value of `U` or of `V`. So another trait may stand between `S` and its listed types. The specification defines "covers" once: a type covers another when every value of the second is a value of the first. The Meet Rule gains a case for closed traits. Where the rule asks for a declaration at the meet of two overloads' parameter types, several declarations below both serve, if together they cover the meet. So a call whose argument's static type stands between closed traits and their listed types may have several most specific declarations. The call's type is the intersection of their return types, and the declaration that runs is unique only at run time. The compiled checker uses coverage only in its overloading rules, to accept an overload set and to justify a call's tie among several most specific declarations, and not in its general subtype test. Why: the proof addendum (`reviews/comprises-type-level-proof-addendum.md`) shows this sound for ground declarations, at calls that need no coercion. A ground declaration's types hold no type variable, and `G[\ZZ32\]` is ground. The addendum shows it for coverage used only in that way, and leaves any wider use to a review of its own. A call that needs a coercion is outside the proof too (F-76 gives what the compiled checker does there). A declaration with static parameters, whose instance dispatch must choose at run time, is outside the proof: one instance would have to meet every one of the return types at once. The typing by the intersection is not extended to it, and the specification states that boundary. Rows 543 and 551: the compiled checker gives no call an intersection type where any declaration of the family has static parameters, and walk checks no `comprises` clause declared outside the main component.

POSITIONS.md:39
- P-42 **A type parameter declared without a bound has the implicit bound `Any`, not `Object`.** `Any` holds tuples, functions and `()`, which `Object` does not. The library instantiates its generic containers at tuple types: its arrays indexed by pairs, such as `(ZZ32,ZZ32)`, are among them. The specification states the bound `Any`, with a callout that records that the Working Draft of February 2011 said `Object`. The compiled path departs from it until the switch-over, which ends the departure: while it uses the compiler's prelude, it bounds such a parameter by `Object`, and so refuses a generic instantiated at a tuple (row 412).

POSITIONS.md:58
- P-62 **The `covariant` keyword is future work, off the path to microGPT.** The keyword, with `contravariant`, is the team's 2012 declaration-site variance: under `trait C[\covariant S\]`, a `C[\Dog\]` is a `C[\Animal\]`, as with Scala's `+S`. No library declaration and no line of microGPT uses it. Row 404 records the hole: the compiled checker accepts variance, but the compiled run dies with `IncompatibleClassChangeError`, and walk refuses the program. The future work is declaration-site variance, carried to run time on both paths. When it lands, a rung tries to bring back the specification's sign-refined number types as covariant static parameters. P-80 keeps their design word for word in the specification, marked superseded.

POSITIONS.md:60
- P-147 **An object defines an inherited abstract method when its bodies of that name at narrower parameter types together cover the abstract method's parameter types.** That is, each value of the abstract method's parameter types is a value of one body's parameter types. A `comprises` clause counts as the compiled checker reads it, which is P-60's reading: a closed trait is covered by its listed types. A body at the abstract method's own parameter types is the plain case. This is the team's rule of 2012, in Steele's abstract-method check of the compiled checker and in the Covered rule of the Welterweight calculus (`Papers/Welterweight/`). So the team's `Library/Pairs.fss` and `ProjectFortress/tests/FileConversion.fss` stay valid: an object in each defines an inherited abstract operator once for each type that a `comprises` clause lists. Walk applies the same rule at load, and its earlier allowance of any one narrower body goes. The traits chapter's sentence, which admitted no narrower body, is revised in the specification's revision form (P-96). Row 725: the acceptance of some valid objects whose methods have static parameters of their own, which the checker and walk (row 728) refuse. Row 665: walk's check of generic objects, which its load check skips.

POSITIONS.md:62
- P-149 **An object that inherits an abstract functional method from one trait, and a body for it from a sibling trait, is refused unless it declares the method itself.** In `object O extends { A, B }`, where `A` declares `pick(self)` abstract and `B` gives `pick(self)` a body, `O` must declare its own `pick`. Scala's way, where the sibling trait's body implements the abstract method, is not taken. The compiled checker refuses such an object, as the specification's text and the type group's Welterweight calculus (`Papers/Welterweight/`) require. Walk already refuses it at load, by the Meet Rule for Functional Methods. A trait that declares one method both abstract and with a body, at the same parameter types, is refused too. Why: the revival honors the designers' intent. It changes Fortress's nature only to reconcile a conflict between the earlier and the later designers' choices, and then looks to other languages for how to do it. Here there is no such conflict, and Fortress is not bent to Scala's way for a hypothetical convenience.

A `where` condition on a function's or a method's own static parameters bounds them. The team's commented-out clause `AnyList comprises List[\E\] where [\E\]` becomes live, which clears the type error of `AnyList`'s join `||`; its other operations, `addLeft` and `addRight`, move into `List` (row 799). `SUM`'s fusion with `MAX` and `MIN`, the library's fast path for the maximum or the minimum of sums, stays. Why: a feature with little support in the team's work bends the language beyond what the curator can review. He has such a feature built where the team left enough design intent for it, or where it is on the critical path to running fast compiled. Row 773: the members scoped to the condition, since a member checked under it stays callable where the condition fails. Row 774: walk's half of conditional extension. Row 701: the code generator's half.

## 7. P-146, the reason for the plain signatures (review-queue item 286)

**Old text**

> - P-146 **In a self-typed trait, the compiled checker types `self` in the method bodies as also being the implementing type.** A self-typed trait is a trait `C[\X\]` whose parameter `X` extends `C[\X\]`, such as `Integral[\I extends Integral[\I\]\]`. - Removed: "The method signatures keep the plain trait type, because the proofs of the POPL 2019 paper on multiple dispatch (Park, Hong, Steele and Ryu) assume that no declared type holds a type parameter inside an intersection."
- Added: "The method signatures keep the plain trait type."

**What is false, and what the change alters**

The sentence gives as the reason that a self-typed trait's method signatures keep the plain trait type that "the proofs of the POPL 2019 paper ... assume that no declared type holds a type parameter inside an intersection". The review of 2026-10-23 found that this assumption is the paper's lemma on matching types at run-time dispatch, which bears on whether the compiled dispatcher is complete, not on the static exclusion test where the vectors' pair had failed, and the phase 3 exit judgement confirms it (section 3.2, item 5). The reason is not his: he said that the option "is more in line with weak signal from repo and has precedent in other languages" (23:32 UTC on 2026-10-13), and the paper's assumption came from the coordinator's ask before his "1.". So, by his rule, the reason goes to the history, and the decision stays: the signatures keep the plain type, and only the exclusion test reads the intersection (the next sentence, P-157).

Nothing built changes. A worker who meets the signature half no longer reads it as forced by the paper; Appendix I keeps the two reasons with their limits, specificity and the Return Type Rule (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex:4058-4073`). The other way is the judgement's own text, which puts a new reason in place of the old: the signatures keep the plain type "for specificity and the Return Type Rule as the conservative choice until phase 5's dispatcher is built". That reason is the judge's, not his, and it names a phase of the plan, which an entry does not hold; so the draft leaves it out. If he wants a reason kept in the entry, that text is the one to take.

## 2. P-45, the pairs on which walk and the checker disagree (review-queue item 296)

**Old text**

> - P-45 **Overloaded declarations may differ in their static parameters.** The specification drops its sentence that forbids this, and keeps it as superseded text. It states instead the overloading model of the type group's 2011 paper (`Papers/Types/`), which the compiled checker already used. The checker keeps the paper's three rules: No Duplicates, Meet and Return Type. It checks the Return Type Rule over every instance of a generic declaration that the argument types allow, not over one guessed instance. One rule of the old sentence survives: if one generic declaration is more specific than another, their static parameters must line up position by position, as Java's rule for overriding a generic method requires. The compiled checker tests it only where the two declarations have as many static parameters of their own (F-75). Walk chooses among overloads by the parameter types that each declaration declares, not by the order in which they are written. At load, walk judges each pair of two generic declarations by the checker's rules on their declared parameter types. It does not refuse a pair only because none of their parameter types exclude, as when one declaration is more specific than the other. Walk and the checker must accept the same pairs. The library repairs, by declarations of its own, the overload sets that the checker refused, and no line of microGPT's two programs changes. Where walk or the checker still judges a pair against these rules: walk compares two functional methods of a generic trait or object on the instance that a call makes (F-26); both paths refuse the paper's own valid example (row 539); walk refuses two generic functional methods of a trait without static parameters whose declared domains lie one inside the other, and fails at a call on su

**The change**

- Removed: "and walk and the checker disagree on four kinds of pair (rows 759 and 786 to 788)."
- Added: "and walk and the checker disagree on three kinds of pair (rows 786 to 788)."

**What is false, and what the change alters**

The last clause counts four kinds of pair on which walk and the checker disagree, row 759 among them. Row 759 is closed: under the compile command's bound `Any`, the checker refuses `g[\T\](a: T)` beside `g(a: Any)`, whose declared domains are equal, as walk does, 'There are multiple declarations of g with the same parameter type: T' (`ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/XXXNoDuplicatesRuleUnboundedBesideAny.test`, a test that expects the refusal; F-274). Rows 786 to 788 stay open, so three kinds remain.

Nothing built changes. A worker no longer looks for a disagreement on that pair. The entry's other rows (539, 779 and 780) are open, as it says.
